Sūt igit mōachi carnales infine regiōis cultores nō solū male inordīati ad aīam: sed etiā ad substantiā monasterij tem<Gap reason="damaged" extent="ca. 1-2 words"/></Line> </Initial>

takes [unclear] upon himself; boldness in sinning is born, because he who despises the authority of correction already commits all crimes as though lawfully. The love of God voluntarily restrains good cenobites from sins, and fear restrains the weak. But where neither the love of God nor fear of correction penetrates the monk, then the mind, through rebellion and the habit of sinning, draws near to hell. For Scripture says: When the impious man has come into the depth of evils, he shows contempt. What does he contemn? He contemns God, despises men, and does not know how to seek the salvation of his own soul.

Therefore he falls into the twelfth degree of pride who, through boldness in sinning, runs into an evil habit. This is the nearest descent to hell; this is the path of hell; this is the swift road to the region covered with the darkness of death. Whoever has once fallen into this degree of the habit of sinning rises again only by the strong hand of the merciful God, because when he does not resist habit, the necessity of sinning is born. For wickedness always advances toward the worse, and as it is always falling it falls more deeply.

Behold, these are the twelve degrees of pride, through which one descends to hell; whoever desires to escape them should always take care to guard himself in the observance of humility. In these twelve evils every unworthiness of vices darkens the cenobite, causes the disordered monk to turn toward himself, and in his morals changes a man into a most savage beast. The end of these things is destruction, and unless before the death of the flesh the remedy of penitence intervenes, the progression of evil degrees condemns the monk to burn without end. But whoever, disordered toward himself, has once fallen into the first degree of pride, unless he strives to rise through penitence from all of it, soon casts himself headlong into the second and consequently into all the rest in order. The sum of the disorder of carnal monks toward themselves is expressed in these degrees of exaltation, through which they show themselves to be disordered citizens of the lowest region. But what we have said about the disordered and proud monk, we must also understand concerning the prelates of the lowest region.

In what manner the citizens of the lowest region [are disordered]. Article VI.

Whoever, established in a monastery, neglects to order his inner affections to the purity of his holy purpose frequently also exceeds measure enormously in outward things. For monks disordered toward God are consequently deemed disordered toward all things. For just as a good cenobite, united to the divine will through love, considers all things according to the right rule of the order with a simple eye, so one turned away from God through disordered affections sins even in the good things which he uses badly. Therefore carnal monks, cultivators of the lowest region, are not only badly disordered toward the soul, but also toward the substance of the monastery

[unclear]. For upon inward confusion in the mind there follows outward disturbance of the body, and the one is shown by the other.

And first, indeed, with regard to the property of the monastery, the citizens of the lowest region are badly ordered when they demand that these things be granted to them in improper order, or by any means usurp more than the usage of regular institution permits. For our Rule commands that all necessary things be given to monks; it utterly forbids superfluous things.

Second, those make bad use of the property of the monastery who do not fear to give and receive contrary to the master’s prohibition, or who, in things entrusted to them, faithlessly commit deceit and fraud. For a monk who, at his own pleasure, without reasonable cause, contrary to the Rule, in any way dissipates the property of the monastery without permission, sins against the Rule like an unfaithful proprietor and a falsifier.

Third, monks or abbots show themselves disordered with regard to the property of the monastery when they indulge in unlawful uses and commit theft and sacrilege, since they turn the property of the monastery to illicit uses. For the substance of the monastery, dedicated to God, is commanded to be guarded like the vessels of the holy altar, lest it be dissipated in any way through negligence. But he who forbids the goods of cloistered persons to be spent uselessly would by no means grant that they be disbursed for sin into shameful uses. What account, then, will monks and rectors of the lowest region owe to our lawgiver in the strict examination, who do not fear to dissipate the property of the monastery upon parents, kinsmen, mimes, actors, and shameful men as an occasion and reward of sin?

Fourth, carnal abbots and monks sin gravely with regard to the property of the monastery, who, to the detriment of divine charity and their own salvation, gather these things together too greedily. For, inflamed by the torches of avarice, they think of nothing but profits and money. Violating feast days, they do not observe them. They always desire to increase temporal goods. They do not notice the losses of charity. They grieve more for a dying beast than for a perishing sinner. Indeed, all these disordered cloistered persons are so blind that they consider avarice to be prudence and think riches to be reform. They join field to field; they call gain piety; and where they see temporal goods abounding, there they say that the best discipline is being observed. They refuse to expend even a few things for the common good of the order, because inwardly they have lost the order of true charity. They raise useless, ostentatious, and damnable structures on high. They buy precious vestments and ornaments less necessary for divine services. They clothe sacred things in gold and leave the poor of Christ naked. This avaricious ostentation does not befit monks, since we who are commanded to imitate the holy men of old are ordered to sell these things for the support of the poor. But a covetous monk and an avaricious abbot are as far from the purpose of holy religion as the devil is from heaven.

Fifth, carnal monks sin with regard to the property of the monastery when they do not repay it with prayers. The alms of the faithful

[They] cheerfully receive [unclear], but few render to the givers the suffrages of prayers. Of these, many citizens of the lowest region, when they have come to the order, serve not God but the belly: they desire that more food, drink, and clothing be given them than necessity requires, and those who in the world could scarcely have bread and vegetables for food, now, having become monks, refuse eggs and little fish.

They importunately demand that large, varied, diverse, and delicate fish be given them; murmuring because of desire for flesh with the children of Israel in the desert, they cry out to their leader; they assert that they cannot eat eggs and peas. They always desire more delicate things.

How the citizens of the lowest region are ill ordered toward contempt of the world.

Article VII.

The kingdom of God suffers violence, and the violent seize it. Therefore whoever desires to enter the heavenly kingdom by the weapons of holy obedience, whoever wishes to live to God under regular conduct, must do violence to the pleasures of the flesh and strongly despise the world with all its vanities. But carnal monks, citizens of the lowest region, who are ill ordered both toward God and toward the goads, are also ill ordered toward contempt of the world.

And first, indeed, they are infected by the concupiscence of the flesh, because they are always burning with the fire of pleasure. In food and drink they are found excessive; in little beds and baths, delicate contrary to the rule. They prefer the desires of the flesh to the salvation of the soul; they do not seek the sweetness of inward conversion. They nourish their flesh too delicately, through which they continually blaze up in various desires. For no one can truly despise the world who neglects to restrain the appetite of the flesh even in the smallest things. If you eat to satiety, you do not truly despise the world. For the first commandment that is imposed on those who despise the world is established in abstinence. But if you fill your belly with food all the way to satiety, at once you fall either into lust or into heavy sloth. Therefore the concupiscence of the flesh draws back the mind of the disordered cenobite, so that he cannot despise the world.

Second, they are ill ordered toward despising the age because of the vain concupiscence of the eyes. For the monk who forgets the true honor of faithful souls takes delight in worldly pomp and altogether curious ornaments. Indeed, each person’s outward apparel reveals what sort of thing lies hidden within him before himself. To carry rings about on the fingers, corals on scarves, little scent-bottles in the hands, and pleats on cowls does not show a monk, but a soldier; it presents not a humble cenobite but a proud secular man. This adornment in monks cannot please others

which to the reprobate; which also is often found to have displeased the proud. Woe to you, disordered cloistered men, who through a double concupiscence of the eyes descend to hell: while you desire to see in others what is not expedient, and present yourselves to be seen by the rest otherwise than you ought. What are the jewels of the age to you? What the curiosities of the world? These beauties, as the blessed Bernard bears witness, quickly effeminate the masculine soul; these worldly dignities quickly enervate a manly purpose. You are like those ragged boys who, because of a single narrow red band fastened to a torn sleeve, consider themselves very handsome and comely, and insolently mock others set before them, though excellently clothed, as if they were naked. These pompous cloistered men see others going about in humble dress, scorning the world in the spirit of poverty, and for that reason pleasing both God and men; but they see themselves despised by the wise and by princes, and sometimes not even admitted to conversation. Seeing these things, the proud, although they grieve heavily as if at an injury, nevertheless utterly refuse to lay aside their haughtiness.

Third, the citizens of the lowest region are badly ordered toward contempt of the world because of pride of life, since they are not only infected with vain complacencies of the flesh, but are also proud through swelling of mind. For those who follow the desires of the flesh vainly lift themselves above themselves; they despise others, however much better than themselves; they do not know how to endure equals; they do not acknowledge superiors. These men rejoice that a great retinue of servants attends them; in councils they strive to sit first; they desire to be seen by all as glorious; they go through public places pompously. Swollen with the spirit of pride, they boast that their monasteries possess, by foundation, insignia opulent in temporal goods, jewels, buildings, and curious privileges. With uplifted heart they despise poor monks or abbots of small monasteries; they do not blush to prefer themselves to better men; and the more they desire to hunt for glory in external things, the more they withdraw with the foolish virgins from true glory.

How the citizens of this lowest region are disordered toward penance.

Article VIII.

Since no one living in time and filled with many miseries can remain long in the same state, it is necessary that, by reforming himself daily with all zeal, he turn himself toward the end that is due, since for as long as anyone is permitted to live in this world, he is considered changeable in either direction. Therefore whoever, established in this changeableness, desires to come to the joys of immutability, let him humbly acknowledge his own frailty, and especially after the fall of sin let him flee to the remedies of penance, and let him fear to lie in crime even for a moment. For the life of a monk ought always to consist in saving penance, and in holy fear [unclear] the coming of the judge C. iii.

to await continually. For blessed Jerome says: “The monk has the office not of one who teaches, but of one who laments: one who should mourn either himself or the world, and, fearful, wait for the coming of the Lord.” But the disorderly cloistered men of the lowest region despise this saving remedy; they consume the acceptable time in vanity; and those who do not fear to be ill-ordered in all things show themselves also very disorderly in doing penance.

First, indeed, they are ill-ordered for penance through carelessness of mind, when they neglect to understand how much sin displeases almighty God, against whom they do not fear to act in contradiction by the choice of a depraved will. As black night is set against day, so the sinner, turned away from the divine goodness, is regarded as hostile and adversarial. What a putrid corpse is wont to do in the sight of human beings, this, in its own way, sin does incomparably in the sight of the angels. But carnal monks despise the honor of God, and therefore do not notice the insult of sin. They neglect to amend venial sins, who as if lawfully commit mortal sins. For Scripture says: “He who neglects little things will fall little by little.” Hence the saying of Bernard admonishes us, saying: “Let no one, brothers, say in his heart: ‘These are light things; I do not care to correct them. It is no great thing if I remain in these venial and very small sins.’ This, brothers, is impenitence; this is the unforgivable blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. For no one can escape greater sins if he has scorned to amend lesser ones.” Nothing is worse for the mind than carelessness.

Second, carnal monks, lovers of the lowest region, are exceedingly disorderly for penance, because they do not notice the contagion of sin. For just as from a contagious disease a healthy person is very often infected, so from one sin a person is inclined into another. For one sin is always said to dispose toward another, unless it is amended as soon as possible through contrition. For the prophet says: “Jerusalem has sinned a sin; therefore she has been made unstable.” And elsewhere: “He who is in filth, let him grow filthy still.” We have, moreover, sufficiently shown this contagion of monks in the degrees of pride; for just as we said that one always arises from another, so we perceive that through carelessness a person becomes slippery from one sin into another.

Third, carnal monks are disorderly for penance because they contract a very bad sickness through the habit of sin, when they incur a destructive blindness of mind. For a vice often committed is slighted, and through habit is judged more lightly. Just as grace enlightens the mind, so frequent transgression blinds reason. For it is written: “Blind the heart of this people and make its ears heavy, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand, lest they be converted and I heal them,” says the Lord. For when the impious man has come into the depth of evils, he despises. No sin is so great that it does not seem light and small through habit.

Fourth, disorderly cloistered men, through the habit of evil,

[unclear] do not come to the grace of true compunction; they approach confession only superficially, from habit; they do not forsake their depraved will; they do not truly take up the purpose of amendment. Woe to those who, buried in the habit of sin, do not fear the censure of strict examination; who do not depart from the blindness of mind through the remedy of contrition, since just as now they despise the long-suffering of God’s goodness, so in that terrible hour they will undergo the sentence of eternal death. What will confession of the mouth be able to profit, where there is no true contrition of the heart? Without contrition there is no saving confession, nor can there be contrition without a purpose of amendment. The sign of contrition is to be unwilling to sin any more.

Fifth, the disordered citizens of the lowest region, having through the habit of sinning become despisers of almighty God, always fall into graver dangers for the soul, while they always approach wickedly the most holy sacred mysteries of the body and blood of the Lord. They make a superficial confession from habit; they allow herds of great vices to run about in their consciences. And now thereafter, as if confederated with hell, they do not fear God; they despise the paths of amendment of life; they think themselves well ordered; though inwardly they are full of vices, they do not care. Sometimes, sensibly affected by a fanciful devotion, they think the Holy Spirit is now present; they affirm that they are beloved of God and holy. They also shamelessly thrust themselves upon the divine mysteries; not discerning the body and blood of the Lord, they take them to themselves unto judgment and condemnation. Finally, such people, communicating unworthily, are more gravely hardened, because, while they think themselves very secure and to be living well, they do not take due care to cleanse their conscience of vices. Thus Judas the apostate, the evil of betrayal which previously, as someone says, he was afraid to carry out against the Savior, after the morsel, when the devil had entered into him, did not fear boldly and without shame to accomplish. O father, many are the citizens of this lowest region: carnal monks, puffed up, proud, envious, murmurers, and afterwards it is effected by various [unclear]; who nevertheless are not afraid to approach the most holy altar almost every day.

Behold, father, the evil company of all who dwell in this lowest region, whose end is destruction, for whom by the death of the body a descent to hell is prepared. This is the far-off region of bestiality and unlikeness, into which that prodigal son went, who squandered the portion of his inheritance luxuriously with harlots. In this region dwell carnal citizens, concerning whom the holy apostle testifies: The animal man does not perceive the things that are of God. In this dark region, deadly and wrapped in the densest darkness, no spiritual good dwells; in it not peace but bestial discord reigns, as the prophet says: There is no peace for the wicked, says my Lord.

Concerning those who are neighbors to this lowest region and very often fall back into it through inconstancy of mind.

Non em̄ spiritus et caro: non ignis et tepiditas in vno domicilio comorant̉: presertim cum tepiditas ipsa soleat domino vomitū ꝓ¬ uocare. Although between the first region of evils and the second of goods there is, properly speaking, no middle place, nevertheless there are some who often move between the two: at one time, through weakness, they are lukewarm; at another, from contrition of mind, they seem to be devout.

These are weak human beings: although they are not submerged in the lowest region, yet through negligence they are very near it, and indeed frequently fall into it through bad habit, since they do not withdraw, as far as they can, from the affections of the flesh. Concerning these Bernard says in a certain sermon: “Lukewarmness is ruinous, because it is dangerous, because it is most troublesome and full of misery and grief; and, being plainly very near to hell, it is rightly reckoned the shadow of death.”

Indeed one may find faint-hearted and slack persons failing under the burden, needing rod and spurs: their joy is slack, their sadness faint-hearted; their compunction is brief and rare. Their thought is animal, their way of life lukewarm; their obedience is without devotion, their speech without circumspection, their prayer without attention of heart, their reading without edification. These, finally, as we see, are scarcely restrained by fear of Gehenna; shame holds them back; reason scarcely bridles them, discipline scarcely checks them. If persons of this sort remain long in this way under the burden, they are either crushed and sink down, or are in some manner in hell, so that they never breathe fully into the light of the Lord’s mercies, nor into the liberty of the spirit, which alone makes the yoke sweet and the burden light.

From this, moreover, such ruinous lukewarmness flows: because their will has not yet been purified, nor do they will the good in the way they know it, being drawn away and enticed by their own concupiscence. For they love in the flesh their earthly little consolations, whether in word, or in sign, or in deed, or in some other thing; and although they sometimes interrupt these things, nevertheless they do not break them off completely. Hence it is that they rarely direct their affections toward God, and their compunction is not continual, but only for an hour. A soul that is subject to these distractions cannot be filled with the visitations of the Lord; and the more it is emptied by the former, the more fully it will be filled by the latter. If much, much; if little, little. Or perhaps, if you approve it more, those former things will never be able to be mingled with these latter for all eternity. For spirit and flesh, fire and lukewarmness, do not dwell in one abode, especially since lukewarmness itself is wont to provoke the Lord to vomit.

Therefore whoever desires to flee from the midst of Babylon, whoever longs to come to the region of the spirit, should take care always to drive torpor of mind away from himself, and, once placed in holiness, to burn continually through the fire of divine love. Nothing is so [unclear] to those who wish to serve as lukewarmness of mind, which always arises at the beginning from a certain small negligence, but, unless it is immediately treated, increases successively in a wonderful way. One established in the neighborhood of the lowest region often slips back into the same, because the dregs of his former fleshly way of life still subtly occupy his will and disturb the weak fervor of devotion on an easy occasion.

But no one can rise again from the depth of hell with a lukewarm will; no one can overcome a habit without a contrary habit, since, unless a certain violence intervenes, the habit of sinning will always strengthen vice. Rightly, moreover, this lowest region is called hell, for by a certain likeness of disturbance and aversion it is compared to hell. Now after this life there are three dwellings of souls, which receive their citizens, emigrating from this world, from the three regions. For the first dwelling is called hell, and this is compared to the lowest region. For as in hell no order dwells, but perpetual horror, so in this lowest region the fury of the mind, blinded by carnal affections, disturbs all things. In hell all are evil, and in the lowest region nowhere are good men found. Whoever fall down to hell have been from the lowest region. For the lowest region always sends its citizens to the lower world, unless, led by repentance, while living they have taken care to renounce dead works.

The second dwelling is called purgatory, and this is compared to the second region, the rational. For just as purgatory purges and perfects souls, and sends them, once purged, to the kingdom of heaven, so this second region washes its citizens, persevering in it through continual exercise, from the filth of sins, and disposes them for ascent to the third region, which is called spirit. In this dwelling all are good, but still to be purged so that they may become better; and in the second region none are evil, but nevertheless they are always exercised so that they may be made better. This region sends its citizens, dying in it, to purgatory, since, even if all are good, nevertheless they do not yet seem fit for the kingdom without temporal purgation. For indeed those who inhabit this middle region, although they appear to be very near the highest, nevertheless are not yet wholly removed from the dust of the lower one. But the third dwelling of separated souls is called the kingdom of heaven, and this is compared to the highest region of the spirit. For as in that heavenly fatherland there is the highest rest and eternal peace, so in the region of the spirit there is continual tranquility of mind.

Here ends the first region.

Preface to the second treatise of the first part, because it deals with the middle region, namely the rational region of cloistered persons.

[unclear] let us hasten. We must go out from the Egypt of the darksome region; we must hasten diligently, through the middle region of reason, to the highest summit of the spirit. Let us therefore now at last enter upon the middle region of the soul, through which one comes by stages to the highest. This region of the soul is quite fittingly called rational, in which continual labor is undertaken for the investigation of the highest truth. The fervor of mind of the citizens of this middle region always strives to raise them to higher things, but the weakness of the flesh, through the motions of a raging storm, tries to drag them back to the lowest things. Hence continual labor; hence sighs and groans arise, because the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and earthly habitation depresses the thinking mind. This is the narrow way that leads to life, and few walk by it. In this region force is imposed upon the concupiscences of the flesh until the will is subjected to the spirit at its nod. For the Lord says in the Gospel: The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it. In that region the war of contest is proclaimed to those who are to serve God. Thus the wise man testifies: Son, he says, when you come to the service of God, stand in fear, and prepare your soul for temptation. How great the temptations are in this middle region we learn daily through the difficulty of spiritual exercise, while, driven in various ways, we cannot remain long in fervor of spirit. Now the weakness of the flesh recalls us from zeal for advancement; now the temptation of the ancient enemy vexes us; now the company of neighbors hinders us. There is need of the greatest fortitude, because no one can resist his temptations unto the end unless he studies daily to do violence to himself. But whoever thinks that he has come to this region should not presume upon his own powers, because just as the grace of God, in order to work good in us, requires the choice of our will, so the will necessarily requires grace. For no one is holy by his own powers. Therefore let no one dare presume upon himself, but let him who stands take care lest he fall. The life of man upon earth is warfare, because one comes to the kingdom through many tribulations, and heaven is acquired by the arduous labors of virtues. The prophet says: Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds; but coming, they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves. Indeed, those who sow in tears shall reap in joy. But if anyone fails in sowing, certainly he will not rejoice in the harvest. Therefore, since through the continual labors of spiritual exercise the mind must be cleansed from the dust of the first region, do not seek leisure in this middle region; do not love the quiet of negligence, because no one is able to stand here except the one who strongly girds himself for continual labor. Whoever in this middle region does not always advance toward better things soon falls back into the negligences of his former life, and there falls into the danger of failing where he has lost the desire of advancing. This is the place of continual contest, in which he who neglects to fight retreats, to be conquered. The preface ends.

Here begins the second region of the soul, which is called rational, in which human beings are engaged amid many labors.

The second region of the soul, therefore, is called rational; in it the mind is exercised in continual labor for the inquiry into supreme truth, and the farther it separates itself from the lowest region, the more it approaches the highest. And this region is set forth as resembling, in certain ways, the ethereal heaven, in which the position of the stars and their continual motion are found. For just as motion itself is disposed in heaven by the order of the first mover, with [unclear] as cause, so continual labor is employed in the middle region, so that each intellectual power may perfect its own object and in no way withdraw from the order naturally assigned to it. The powers of the soul of this kind are three: memory, intellect, and will.

Of these, memory gathers the likenesses of things and phantasms, and extends itself toward the difficult. The intellect, by discerning those phantasms themselves, considers them, and here investigates the true. The will embraces what has been approved by the intellect in due order, and this is occupied with the known good. When these three powers of the soul rightly preserve their order, they lead the spirit in faith to heavenly things.

This second region, moreover, is compared to the ethereal heaven, in which, just as there is continual motion and the position of the stars, so in this middle region there is continual motion and labor against the contests of vices. And just as the motion of the stars, by the order of its office implanted in it by nature, accomplishes its task, so also in this region the equity of rectitude is required to come about, so that each power of the soul, while it is subjected to its own object, may be perfected to the ordained end assigned to it, so far as can befall wayfarers. For not simply can any of these powers be perfected to fullness in this region, since no one in this pilgrimage is so perfect that he cannot be more perfect in his own order. For even if memory, in its own object, which is the difficult, could behold the gathered likenesses and phantasms of all creatures, nevertheless it would not be satisfied unless it could apprehend their beginning, which is God. But this is altogether impossible for this region, in which we can form no phantasms or likenesses concerning God. The intellect also, the counsellor, so to speak, of the blind will, extends itself toward the true; but however much it considers its own object, it is not satisfied until it can apprehend all truth and come to knowledge of the eternal, supreme, and ineffable truth without the opinion of fantastic speculation. But that perfection is possible for no wayfarer so long as mortality is present in the mortal body. The will also, in its own object, which is the good, [unclear] to be satisfied and

[unclear] will not be able to rejoice unless it reaches that unchangeable and highest good, which no instability of change overshadows. The highest truth and unchangeable good is God, who said to Moses: “No man shall see me and live.” And the disciple of the highest truth says: “No one has ever seen God.” But the prophet too, addressing the Lord, says: “Truly you are a hidden God.” Although the aforesaid three powers of the soul cannot perfectly comprehend their object in this life, nevertheless none of them ought to cease from its office, lest it incur the danger of failing precisely where it has laid aside the practice of striving. Therefore the citizens of this middle region mortify evil affections in themselves; they adorn themselves with constant virtues; they direct all their works with right intention; they depart not at all from the office of reason.

But the citizens of this region are scholastic men, speculative and active, devoted to various and indeed honorable arts, who subject the sensual or carnal powers to reason; who do not cease to cleanse these three powers of the soul from all unlawful objects; who always lift their intention toward the end of honorable usefulness; who reform the will, in act or in habit, toward its due end. Therefore the monk who loves purification and desires to ascend in spirit to the third region ought to observe the following principal articles, which stand in the middle region.

The summary of the truth of this middle region is expressed in seven principal articles.

Whoever in this middle region desires to advance according to the vow of his profession should take diligent care to observe the following articles. If he neglects to keep them, he shows that he is still not a citizen of the middle region, but of the lowest. For, as we said above, no one can remain in this middle region without a continual effort to make progress; in it, not to have advanced is to fail, and not to have ascended is to descend. Therefore the monk who, having overcome the dark region, has at last, with the Lord’s help, deserved to reach this middle one, should know that he must take care not to abandon, even for a little, the effort to make progress, but always stretch himself toward further things; and let him remember the admonition of the wise man, who says: “Unless you hold yourself constantly in the fear of the Lord, your house,” that is, your conscience, “will quickly be overthrown.” For it is impossible for anyone to advance in holy conduct if he neglects daily to renew the effort of progress through the fear of the Lord. The effect of this renewal is then shown to be ordered when the truth of the articles of the middle region is duly observed. The first article, therefore, is diligent attention to the cenobitic end. The second is the due restraint of the sensual powers

[unclear]tion. The third is the faithful cleansing of the powers. The fourth is the attentive reformation of works at the end of the region. The fifth is the ordered institution of true cenobitic progress. The sixth is the adaptation of the powers for entry into the third region; and the seventh is the exemplary or experimental certainty of all the things aforesaid.

On the continual and diligent intention of the end of cenobitic life.

Article I.

Since the end is first in the intention of the wise person, and each thing in its own kind is judged the more perfect the more it approaches its end, the monk who cultivates this middle region should always consider why he has entered religion; and if he finds his intention well ordered, he should strive to continue it. But if he finds it corrupted, he should not neglect to reform it to the rectitude of the end that is due.

But note that in spiritual exercises the end is described as twofold, through which the virtue of monastic life is increased in merits. The first is charity, which is called principal and ultimate; to it all monastic exercises are ordered as to a first cause. Whatever good we do must always and principally be ordered to this end, because no work of virtue receives merit unless charity always lays the due foundation. “God,” says John, “is charity; and he who abides in charity abides in God, and God in him.” But he who abides in God does not sin. The second end, disposing toward the first principal end, is directed as it were through some fitting means; and this is called secondary, or less principal. The monk must always attend to this end, and through it order his exercises to the ultimate end. For no one can reach the principal end of charity who neglects to observe the means.

This disposing end, however, in relation to the ultimate end, so far as it pertains to cenobites, according to John Cassian in the Conferences of the Fathers, is to cast away from oneself entirely all cares of the world, to mortify one’s own wills, to entrust every disposition and care of oneself to the superior, and to think nothing of tomorrow. For a cenobite who wishes to make progress in this middle region must assume the complete denial of himself, and then resign himself totally into the hands of his superior, so that within himself he may be inwardly free from every secular occupation. Indeed, unless our cenobite has arrived at this end, he is by no means a true monk, because he still sows corruption in corruptible flesh and in no way observes the virtue of his profession.

This denial of monastic self-will, however, seems principally to consist in three things, without which no one can truthfully say himself

[unclear] is to have renounced. And first indeed, the mortification of one’s own will requires in a monk the eradication of his own judgment; for whoever relies on his own judgment or counsel disdains humbly to be subject to another. For the root from which the defense of one’s own will arises is called attachment to one’s own counsel or judgment. But whoever, placed in a monastery, desires to cling to his own judgment, sins gravely against the Rule as a usurper of his own will. For it befits a cenobite rather to live under another’s command, if he desires to arrive at eternal life through the merit of obedience. Indeed, to love one’s own judgment is the greatest leprosy of the soul, which, according to Bernard, is the more pernicious the more hidden it is; because the more someone abounds in it, the healthier he seems to himself to be. Secondly, the mortification of the will requires the emptying out of one’s own affections, since no one is able to stand ordered among adverse and favorable things and truly subject to God who does not firmly restrain his carnal affections. Thirdly, for the mortification of one’s own will that poverty of spirit is required, lest in usable things, food, clothing, and the rest, the monk’s affection be held captive; for whoever loves these things too much shows himself, contrary to the Rule, to be a lover of his own will. For it is fitting that the true cenobite, inhabitant of this middle region, earnestly devote himself to the teaching of holy humility, willingly despise all worldly things for love of God, and love absolutely nothing except God. If he has anything for his use with the Rule permitting it, let him beware of attaching the affection of his heart to it; and let him be ready, at the pastor’s decision and for the usefulness of the brethren, to resign all things with a peaceful heart. Let him always choose the simpler and meaner things; let him give thanks to God in all things, placing his hope and his sufficiency in him alone, and let him say cheerfully: In you, Lord Jesus, possessing all things, for your love I willingly despise all things; concerning transitory things, nothing at all

Therefore let our devout cenobite always direct the eye of his intention, with faithful consideration, to this end of the institution of the monastic [unclear]. Let him never depart from its [unclear]. For whoever in action forgets the ultimate end wanders like an unskilled and blind sailor amid the storms of the sea, soon to perish. Therefore let the faithful monk imitate a sailor skilled through devotion, so that, just as he, always having the harbor before his eyes, strives with intent solicitude to steer the ship thither, so the mind of a good man may always be directed to God as to the shore and the ultimate end. Archers set up for themselves some fixed mark, and, lest their sight be scattered from the appointed limit, they close one eye. And just as the arrow of the shooter is directed to the mark, so the intention of the good monk is always ordered toward God; in it also the eye of lower action is closed, lest the sharpness of higher contemplation be scattered through vain things. For it is necessary [unclear] the affection of earthly curiosity and the understanding of carnal wisdom as though

[unclear]: if with the gaze of the mind we always desire to raise [ourselves] to the proper end. And just as the eagle is said to look upon the sun with undazzled eyes, so the monk, the servant of God, contemplates without interruption the end of the monastic institution. Just as a prudent traveler, as he proceeds pleasantly, keeps in view the lodging toward which he is making his way, so the good cenobite, in everything that he does, always with fervent desire chiefly longs for his end, which is God. But foolish is the traveler who, set upon the road, forgets the lodging toward which he is tending, and, wandering off elsewhere, knowingly entangles himself in various hindrances. And the monk who does not earnestly keep in view the end of his destination is indeed wandering blind upon the road.

Therefore the good monk, and lover of his own salvation, does not neglect his good striving in spiritual exercises, but always lifts up his affection toward higher things by exercising himself in holy works. Good striving, moreover, is to omit nothing of the things that God has commanded; for love of God to obey the pastor humbly in all things; always to lift up one's affection, withdrawn from earthly things, to the memory of heavenly things; and through the continual exercise of spiritual conduct to renew the holy purpose every day. Whatever good the devout cenobite does, let him always offer it to almighty God with faithful attention; let him despise all earthly things with a strong spirit; let him desire to please God alone.

Let the intention of the faithful cenobite always be that he wish to desire nothing other than the praise and honor of God; let his attention be diligent, so that he knows how to summon all the senses of the body and the affections of the soul to the service of God, in order that he may serve his Lord faithfully and seek his glory, not his own.

On the Due Restraint of the Sensual Powers. Article II.

How useful and also how necessary it is for us to restrain [them], especially among monks, I think no one is ignorant. Truly, whoever desires to reach, in this region, the proper end of regular conduct that we have described must tame, with prudent constancy, both his disordered natural habits and impulses, because no one can truly suffice to resign himself to another's authority who does not strongly restrain the powers of the sensual passions. For it is necessary for the one who desires to make progress to leave behind both the impulses and the prudence of the flesh with steadfast spirit, and to show himself a son of divine grace, not of flesh and blood. For Scripture says: “If you live according to the flesh, you will die.” Truly, those who sow in the flesh will also reap corruption from the flesh.

Caro autem et sanguis regnum dei non possidebunt. Sed quidam de nobis saluator? Inimici inquantum homines domestici eius sunt. Et quoque si isti domestici nisi vires sensuales quam spiritui aduersantur? Concupiscibilitas enim et irascibilitas inimici nostrorum oĩa in nobis mala adversus spirituum concitant: et domum consciencie varijs passionibus continue perturbant. Quandiu emendate vires sensuales suos naturales motus et cursus in hoĩe pagunt: ipsum ad libertatem spūs ascēdere non permittunt. Concupiscibilitas in sensualiter carnis delectabilis fruitur: et vis e contrario irascibilis penalia corporalis detestatur. Interea quando diu hoc bellum carnis in hoĩe agitur: inquietus carnis et infime regionis cultor monachus habetur. Quicunquę ergo venire ad vitam eternam desiderat: necessesse est vt has inordinatas sensualium vires fortiter in omnibus restringat. ¶ Studeat ergo cenobita fidelis vim concupiscibilem ad penalia que deo stultis accepta dirigere. et oẽs suas affectões ad dei bonum placitum reformare. Si hoc fecerit: confidenter ad dominum orabit. Concupiuit anima mea desiderare iustificaciones tuas in omni tempore. Et illud sepius dulciter lachrymando clamabit. Quemadmodum desiderat ceruius ad fontes aquarum? ita desiderat aīa mea ad te Deus. Deinde vim irascibilem deo adherens delectationibis sensualibus prudenter opponere: ea quodlibet ad vitioque ordinatum sedulo reformare. Sic animum ad suum ordinationem principium dura quequaque dei amore non metuet appetitur: et oĩbus consupiscientes carnalibus fortiter per vim irascibilem incipiet reluctari. Et tunc cenobita devoteus eleuans se spū clamabit. Renuit solari aīa mea. Et illud apl̃ti. Dia arbitratius sum vt sertorora. Aīa emendate que deum veraciter diligit: omnia preter ipsum contemnit. ¶ Ex his autem duabus viribus oĩs affectio ĩordinata oritur: et bone stultorum opposicionum hoc generantur. Nam de concupiscibili gaudiuum et spesis summum exordium. et irascibilis dolorē parturit et metum. De his scutum ita dicit Bernardus. Totum cor hoĩs quattuor affectionibus est peruersum quas si ad deum reducimus: totum cor hominis est conuersum. De fidelitate mundatione. Articulus iij. Sed restringere vires sensuales nequaquam sufficiens nisi etiam potestatis intellectuales fideliter emundare. Ad hanc emundationem magna et continua diligencia opus est. Quia enim negligencia corruptore resolutur: nunquam a vitiosis corruptiones emundatur. Qui enim corruptis potestates seminat: nihil aliud quam corruptionem de suis erroribus reportat.

Flesh and blood, however, shall not possess the kingdom of God. But what [does] the Savior [say] to us? A man’s enemies are those of his own household. And who are these household members, if not the sensual powers that are opposed to the spirit? For concupiscibility and irascibility, enemies of our [unclear], stir up in us all evils against the spirit, and continually disturb the house of conscience with various passions. As long as the [unclear] sensual powers carry out their natural movements and courses in a man, they do not permit him to ascend to the liberty of the spirit. Concupiscibility sensually enjoys the delights of the flesh; and, on the contrary, the irascible power detests bodily pains. Meanwhile, when this war of the flesh is long waged in a man, he is regarded as a restless monk, a cultivator of the flesh and of the lowest region. Therefore whoever desires to come to eternal life must strongly restrain in all things these disordered powers of the senses.

Therefore let the faithful cenobite strive to direct the concupiscible power toward the painful things which are [unclear] acceptable to God, and to reform all his affections according to God’s good pleasure. If he does this, he will pray confidently to the Lord: “My soul has longed to desire your justifications at all times.” And often, weeping sweetly, he will cry out that other verse: “As the hart longs for the springs of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God.” Then, cleaving to God, let him prudently set the irascible power against sensual delights, and diligently reform whatever in it is ordered toward vice. Thus he will not fear the soul’s hard return to its first ordering for the love of God, and by means of the irascible power he will begin strongly to resist all carnal things that stir up desire. And then the devout cenobite, raising himself in spirit, will cry out: “My soul refused to be comforted.” And that saying of the Apostle: “I have judged [unclear] as dung.” The amended soul that truly loves God despises all things except him.

From these two powers, however, every disordered affection arises, and from this the [unclear] oppositions of [unclear] are generated. For from the concupiscible power joy and hope take their highest beginning, and the irascible power gives birth to sorrow and fear. Of these the shield [unclear] Bernard says thus: “The whole heart of man is perverted by four affections; if we bring these back to God, the whole heart of man is converted.”

On faithful cleansing. Article 3. But it is by no means enough to restrain the sensual powers unless one also faithfully cleanses the intellectual powers. For this cleansing great and continual diligence is needed. For because by negligence [unclear] is dissolved, it is never cleansed from vicious corruptions. For he who sows in corrupted powers reports back nothing other than corruption from his errors.

Therefore it is necessary for the cenobite, the cultivator of this middle region, to correct his inner powers from every disorder, if he wishes to remain continually in the pursuit of making progress. These intellectual powers, moreover, are to be amended in this way.

First, the intellect must be purged of every imagination of vain likenesses, so that, tearing itself away from all material things, it may raise itself upward, without any imagination of likeness, to its principle; and, prudently intent upon its object, may turn itself wholly toward the ray of supreme truth.

Then let our faithful cenobite not neglect to cleanse his memory from every occupation with illicit things; let him admit no forms of shameful or less useful thoughts; and let him strive to repel the phantasms of irrational passions through holy meditations, and, as far as can be done, to think nothing foolish.

The will also must be purged of every disordered affection, so that it may wish nothing except what right reason suggests is to be wished, and reject nothing except what that reason, according to the judgment of truth, forbids it.

But this restraint of the powers and cleansing of the faculties, as we have said, is granted to no one at all except through great, discreet, and continual diligence in strong combat, knowing that the kingdom of God suffers violence, and that no one can subject the enemy to himself unless he has wished to fight against him fiercely and perseveringly. For, blessed Bishop Augustine bearing witness, we have learned that a man does not die well unless he has first died to vices and desires. But no one truly dies to these among men unless he resists his own wills through continual labor, sowing in tears. The mind, therefore, must be fortified with salutary teachings; strength of patience must be assumed in all things, because [unclear] the enemy with spiritual arms and with a certain continual violence of fighting, he cannot cleanse his intellectual powers. But although the weapons of spiritual warfare are many in its progress, nevertheless three are chiefly to be assumed by the monk.

And first, indeed, vigor is necessary for the cenobite in all that he does, so that he may dare courageously to undertake things contrary to the flesh, and may never at any time grow lukewarm in his holy purpose. For the exercises of the spirit are hard and wholly contrary to the flesh; in them he is not able to persevere constantly who disdains to put on the weapons of the strongest vigor. Therefore, if you desire to subject all your affections to the spirit, if you wish to fight successfully against the vices of the flesh, take care to do yourself a most prudent violence, and to arm yourself strongly against all things.

Then a certain holy severity is proposed to be assumed by you, through which all contrary and adverse things of this world are borne as though they were nothing. Indeed, whoever [unclear] this kindly severity of mind for the love of God

...and with heavenly desire has once truly taken it up: from then on he will now fear no adversities of the flesh, while he is so suffused within by the contemplation of divine reward that he seems to take more delight in adversities than in prosperities that befall him.

But severity is by no means pleasing to the weaker, unless kindness has been tempered somewhat with sweetness. Therefore, accordingly, kindness itself must be taken up by our soldier, so that when, through the weakness of the flesh, tempted in battle or even sometimes wounded, he falters, he may at once rise again through penitence, to fight more strongly anew. For the soldier of Christ, if he has fallen in battle, must rise again as often as necessary, through contrition and the other remedies of penitence, to fight once more, until at last, by God’s mercy, he is able to overcome the adversary. If the just man falls seven times in a day and rises again, how shall the sinner, but now penitent, not hope for pardon? Rise again to fight as often, O soldiers, as you have fallen when the adversary conquered; always renew the warfare afresh more bravely, so that the enemy whom you cannot destroy by strength you may at last overcome by perseverance. Do not despair of victory, O faithful cenobite, because, often conquered by the temptation of vices, you have fallen into the snare. Do not lie prostrate any longer because you feel yourself weak, but rise again at once as often as you have slipped, and trust how merciful a Lord you have; by his help you will at last be victor against the adversary. For no one becomes supreme all at once, nor is victory over the enemy granted immediately to incautious soldiers, lest, to their greater ruin, they be lifted up into pride. The possession of a thing acquired with difficulty is always dearer, and a good that is acquired laboriously is guarded with greater diligence. For so long does God, the kindly Father, permit us, conquered by the temptations of the adversary, to fall by turns into the pit of sin, until, conscious of our weakness, we learn to hope in nothing in our own powers, but only in his grace. But you, man, who have often broken your resolve by sinning, never delay to rise again; for even if you cannot perfectly subject the enemy to yourself, nevertheless it will be good for you if the last day can find you standing and fighting, even after an often repeated fall. But for those to whom the mercy of God has granted strength and grace to conquer the adversary, this counsel does not loosen discipline. Nevertheless, let him who stands take heed lest he fall.

On the careful reformation of the works of the first region.

Since indeed, as we taught at the end of the first treatise, this middle region is nearest to the first from its lowest part, in which, if the cenobite has been even somewhat negligent and slack, he immediately falls back without interval into the former one. And therefore he who is making progress in this region...

wishes to persist: with ever attentive vigilance he should strive to reform the works of the lowest region. And, lest we be too lengthy: whoever desires to exercise this reformation in himself should take up, in this region, works contrary to the eight articles of the first. For, as the tradition of physicians teaches and prescribes: opposites are cured by opposites.

Therefore the citizens of this middle region, faithful monks, are commanded first to consider this: that they should strive before all things to order themselves toward God. This ordering is said to be well made when God is loved with the whole heart, according to the law, above all things.

Next, the devout cenobite should show himself ordered toward his prelate in all things: he should show humility and render reverence; he should strive to love him with sincere charity, and to keep all the things that he commands according to the Rule.

The rector also of souls should take care to walk in ordered fashion toward the cenobites, and to show himself a shepherd to the sheep, not a hireling: he should not neglect the salvation of the souls committed to him; he should not put temporal things before spiritual things. Let him hate vices, love the brothers, and show himself exemplary in all good things.

Then the brothers should cleave to one another like members of one head; in the true charity of God they should love one another mutually and not depart from good zeal. For since we trust that, by the faith of Christ and by applying ourselves to good works, we shall come to eternal life, we are members of Christ, the supreme head. But whoever persecutes his brother with evil zeal or hatred and the other evil affections first divides himself from the head, and then does injury to Christ.

Consequently each person shows himself ordered toward himself: for the love of Christ he should humbly subject himself to all; by humility he should prefer others to himself, and believe himself more unworthy than all the monks.

In the use of the things of the monastery they should always beware of exceeding the institution of the Rule, but should strive to show themselves ordered in all things and faithful everywhere. They should desire to have nothing against the will of the Abbot; they should admit no pleasure of the mind in the use of things.

Next, faithful cenobites will take care to order themselves, according to the regular institution, to contempt of the world, so that they love nothing in this world, but despise all things sincerely for the love of God.

They should not neglect to order themselves most diligently to penance; they should often have recourse to humble confession of their transgressions, because just as no one is believed to live in a place in the world without sin, so penance is judged necessary for all, even for monks. For the good cenobite should always learn, through the study of compunction, to have recourse to penance, and humbly to accuse himself of his transgressions in chapter, gladly to perform the penance enjoined, and faithfully to amend himself in all things.

The greatest virtue of a monk is humility, and the gravest crime in a cenobite is pride. For a monk who is proud with a swollen mind becomes an imitator and servant of the devil; and he is stripped of all virtues, if he had any, because no virtue can subsist in a mind in which pride has happened to dwell. Therefore the cenobite who desires to make progress in this middle region should learn to order himself toward the true advancement of monastic discipline through humility, because no one truly attains humility except one who dwells upon spiritual studies. But true advancement in the regular discipline, excluding all adulterous Muses, arises from the degrees of humility, which are set down as twelve in the Rule through their roots. I say that the roots of this advancement come from the study of sacred reading, which lead a man little by little to the fear of the Lord. From reading arises spiritual meditation; from this holy compunction is born. But the more useful manner of cenobitic meditation consists in the remembrance of the Lord’s Passion and in the consideration of God’s benefits. Further, those who, passing beyond this middle region, come to tranquility of spirit, make their meditations more sublime through contemplation of the divine majesty and excellence. And concerning these we shall speak in their own place. These two roots, moreover, receive their increase from the watering of constant prayer, and grow strong into the strength of a very firm plant. For no meditation profits without prayer, and study without it will not save.

From these three arises spiritual advancement, the fear of the Lord, which is the first degree of humility; from it the other degrees, succeeding in order, are brought forth. But monks who neglect the salutary study of the Scriptures and holy meditations together with constant prayers cannot ascend to this first degree of humility; when will they be able to come to the others? For the second is never ascended if the first is neglected. Therefore he who neglects one ascends none.

The study of sacred reading, however, must not be undertaken by them for the vanity of the world, nor for the pleasure of a seduced mind, because reading never profits toward compunction when the delight of the flesh or of vanity has corrupted it. But a monk cannot attain devotion through the study of sacred reading unless he strives to change all curiosity into a simple spirit. Therefore whoever desires to advance from the reading of the Scriptures to compunction, whoever longs to ascend to humility through the roots of fear, ought not to choose just any subject matter for reading, but only that which can more fully stir the mind to the love of God. For this purpose the reading of the conduct of the saints seems to me sufficiently suitable, because often the mind, as it lies low, is raised up to the love of God when the life of his servants is recalled to memory. [Re]velations of the torments or joys of separated souls, when they are in conformity with the catholic faith, we freely admit; by them we have found that sluggish hearts are very often stirred to compunction. Finally, the passions of the holy martyrs excite in no small measure the fervor of devotion; in them, when we recall to mind the unconquerable charity of Christ, pierced by the example of such constancy and touched as if by a certain fire of love, we sigh over our imperfection. From reading the material for meditation is taken; and such as the former has been, such will the latter be. It is not the shameful songs of poets, not the curious doctrines of philosophers, not the swollen writings of rhetoricians, that excite the fervor of devout compunction in monks; rather, they choke off what has been conceived. If, therefore, you wish to devote yourself to good meditations, do not occupy your soul with other readings than holy and devout ones. For indeed the grape is not gathered from thorns, nor is compunction born from the study of vanities. Let him who studies for the knowledge of this world read those things that are suited to his learning; but let him who seeks compunction think on those things that kindle the soul to the love of God through fear. Therefore let frequent reading take its beginning from the last things that await us; then let the deeds of the holy fathers be read, so that the memory of future things may strike the mind with fear of God, and the exemplary conduct of the saints may kindle the desire to imitate them. For the wise man says: Remember your last things, and you will not sin forever. The conduct of the holy fathers is set before us as an example, and the destruction of the wicked is recounted to us for our discipline, so that rewarded virtue may move desire, and punished iniquity may forbid the license of sinning. Therefore let the devout cenobite always recall to memory the examples and virtues of the saints; let him consider the brief pleasure of the depraved but their eternal torment, so that by fearing unhappiness he may deserve to escape it, and by cleaving to virtues to obtain their perpetual joy. The distinct condition of the good and the wicked is no light matter, since each is described as going to remain forever, and is bounded by no end. O eternity, ever to be feared by all mortals, in which, after this life, there is no fear of condemnation for the just, and no hope of liberation for the perverse. Let him who can think what eternity is; where there is no end, let him who dares imagine a boundary; and when he has found nothing in eternity except eternity, let him understand that all the time in which he lives in this world is nothing. For indeed the spirit, once stripped of the flesh, is necessarily compelled to enter this abyss of eternity, and the condition that it has once obtained according to its merits it will endure without end, and will not exchange for another. For he who dies good in the charity of God will obtain eternal life according to his merit. But he who is evil and, without the reconciliation of penitence, has once departed from this life, will remain to be tormented without end with the demons in hell. From these meditations servile fear arises in the mind, through which one gradually comes to love. But so that the cenobite through these roots

...so that we may be able to lead [them] by stages to charity: it is our pleasure briefly to explain in order the degrees of humility described in the Rule.

First, the fear of God is described, which is called the beginning of wisdom. The fear of the Lord is handed down under a threefold distinction, namely servile, initial, and filial, which is also called chaste. From this threefold distinction three roots are said to proceed, according to which the beginner in the cenobitic life ought to order his meditations. For each root has its own proper meditations; and when one is rightly disposed, another, better one is always generated.

For from servile fear, assumed nevertheless not servilely but prudently and virtuously, there arise meditations of horror and of punishments; these, restraining the soul from sin, gradually introduce filial fear. For indeed, when by consideration of punishments the mind is turned to horror, boldness in sinning is restrained, because the servant who fears blows keeps the Lord's commandments. But this servile fear by itself does not suffice for meriting the paternal inheritance; nevertheless its initial effect disposes one toward filial fear, which is sufficient.

For initial fear is placed between the two, and is easily changed from servile into filial. This initial fear receives meditations concerning the last things, and it dreads both to incur punishments and to lose the sweet homeland. And this is set forth more fully in the Rule, where its roots are also described.

Filial fear, however, embraces its meditations in love, since it fears nothing else except that the beloved father be offended. Of this fear the wise man says: The fear of the Lord is glory and boasting, gladness and a crown of exultation. The fear of the Lord will delight the heart, and will give gladness and joy for length of days. And again: For him who fears God it will be well at the end, and on the day of his death he will be blessed. This fear is also called chaste, because not from fear of punishments but solely from love [unclear] it detests evils.

From this threefold fear we see three breadths of spiritual exercises arise concerning the degrees of humility, and to each fear its own exercises correspond. For servile fear performs its exercises in one way; initial fear applies itself to virtues in another; and filial fear proceeds in its works in a much different way. For just as the affections of hearts arise in varied fashion, so the exercises of a single fear take place in diverse ways. For in one way the publican, mindful of his crimes, feared the sentence of the judge; in another way Jerome said that he heard the voice of the trumpet calling the dead to judgment. For concerning that man the holy Gospel says: Standing far off, the publican would not lift up his eyes to heaven, but striking his breast he said: God, be merciful to me, a sinner. But that blessed Jerome says: Whether I drink or eat, I always think I hear that trumpet sounding in my ears. Sur

“Arise, you dead: come to judgment.” The compunction of both arises from fear, but both are not generated from the desire of one and the same affection. For the publican, terrified by the guilt of his sins, feared the sentence of the just judge, and therefore, being pierced with compunction, said: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” But Jerome is shaken by fear not from the guilt of conscience, but, grounded in charity and reckoning himself an unprofitable servant, reveres the abyss of divine justice.

The second degree is to relinquish one’s own will for the love of God, and in no respect to love one’s own willing contrary to the rule. This degree arises from the first ascent of humility and is raised into the third. For truly, he who fears God and fears to be separated from him, and truly dreads undergoing punishments, hates nothing more than his own will. For the faithful cenobite knows that every sin arises from one’s own will alone, and therefore detests it as the gate of hell. For that blessed man truly said: “Take away one’s own will, and there will no longer be hell.” For nothing burns in hell except one’s own will; nothing loses the grace of God except voluntary fault. Therefore whoever truly fears God and fears losing his grace is afraid of his own will as of an ambusher of his soul. Consideration of the danger of one’s own will makes the cenobite despise his own willing and deny himself to himself. And this denial of one’s own will and of oneself is accomplished in the manner that will be stated in what follows.

First, then, he who denies himself to himself studies to live according to the teaching of eternal wisdom and not according to his own impulses, and to obey Christ in all things as he persuades him by humility. Therefore let the Savior say to the cenobite: “If you wish to deny yourself and follow me, turn your eyes away lest they see harmful things, your ears lest they hear vain things; and in place of the sweet things of this world take bitter things. Learn to despise the pleasures of your body, to love tranquillity and peace of heart, to receive all tribulations for love of me patiently and gladly, and desire to be seen by all as worthless and contemptible. Consequently, learn to break your wills in all things, to mortify your desires, to despise all earthly things, and to conform your life, as far as possible, to the conduct of your Savior according to your strength. For he who says that he remains in Christ ought himself also to walk just as he walked.” Whoever has done these things has well denied himself.

Second, the denial of one’s own will is then rightly accomplished when the advantages of others are set before one’s own. For the holy apostle says: “Not seeking the things that are their own, but the things that are others’.” For according to the saying of Bernard, the soul is laid down for the brethren as often as their advantages are preferred to one’s own benefits for the love of God.

Third, the resignation of one’s own will receives the fullness of perfection when the cenobite, pierced with compunction and wholly made over to God--

[unclear] desires out of love to serve him freely, without regard for reward. And that most holy resignation of one’s own will makes a man very near to God, and he always rests in his love.

For just as this resignation of oneself receives its foundation from the second degree of humility, so too an inward and complete resignation to the will of God in all things is necessarily required. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “I have not come to do my own will, but that of the Father who sent me.” Perfect resignation, therefore, is that by which the human will is wholly subjected to the divine will and conformed to it out of entire love. For thus the Lord himself taught us to pray: “Thy will be done, as in heaven and on earth.” And that saying of the psalm-writer: “Into thy hands I commend my spirit.” No one ever lives securely in this world unless the human will is perfectly subjected to God.

Indeed, the perfect resignation of oneself, by which the cenobite truly subjects his will to God, shows the straight way to the highest without any intermediary. Here there is the greatest tranquility of mind, the greatest security in the heart, since the soul that strives to subject itself perfectly to God will be able to fear no opposition of this world any longer, except sin alone. Whatever adversity comes upon it, with the Lord’s help it has learned to overcome; whatever convenience it desires, it understands that it possesses in the Lord alone. It despises all adverse things for love of him; it has placed all good things in love of him. For that devout man spoke prudently: “Give [unclear] all good things [unclear] has placed in love of him. Forsake cupidity, and you will find true peace.”

Finally, in order that this resignation of one’s own will may receive the fullness of consummation, it implores, so to speak, the support of a threefold assistance.

The first is placed in the virtue of perseverance, so that the will once denied may never be taken back. For against those who despise this assistance that holy Bernard says: “Why do you again take charge of yourselves, you who once, by mature deliberation, handed over your will to us?” For a good monk who has once handed over his will to God into the hands of the abbot does not take it back without the guilt of sacrilege.

The second thing required for the perfect resignation of the will is that it never grow slack. Hence the Lord says to the lukewarm soul in the Apocalypse: “I have a few things against you, because you have abandoned your first charity,” that is, your fervor.

Third, resignation of the will is perfected if it is never cut off. For the Savior says: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved.” Therefore, when you see a cenobite restless or moved to anger, know that the whole mass of the temptation proceeds from lack of resignation; nor will you ever take care of this disease of sickness unless you first persuade him to the resignation of the denied will.

The third degree of humility is to submit oneself in all obedience to a superior for love of God, and to show oneself an imitator of Christ by deeds, not words; concerning this the holy Apostle says: “He became obedient unto death, even death on a cross.” This degree takes its beginning from the second and raises its ascent as far as its own third degree. For just as the second mortifies one’s own will by denying it, so this one lays the foundation of holy work through humble subjection. The former subjects itself wholly to the divine will; this one, for love of God, also obeys men. The keeping of one degree without the observance of the other is not sufficient in a monk, nor is the will of a cenobite subjected to divine ordering if he disdains to obey the command of a superior.

Therefore the true cenobite places all his joy in the virtue of holy obedience. He thinks it the greatest gain to fulfill in all things the will of his shepherd; he believes that he incurs grave loss to his soul if he finds that he has committed even a little outside obedience. For he always considers with faithful devotion what the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who hears you hears me; and he who despises you despises me.” Hence that blessed Bernard says to the monks: Whatever a man commands in God’s place must be received no otherwise than if God himself commanded it in person. Therefore let the true monk prefer this subjection of obedience to every sacrifice; let him do absolutely nothing against its integrity; and let him continually say to himself within himself what is written: “Obedience is better than victims.” Hence the Rule too says: “Therefore all things are to be done with the will of the abbot.”

Now this degree, as we have said, arises from the second. He who, for fear of God, perfectly abandons his own will now seeks nothing else in this world than to follow that will in all things. But because God speaks once and does not repeat the same thing, a weak man cannot know the will of the Most High; for this reason he has committed himself into the hands of his prelate. Therefore let the cenobite obey, according to the Rule, the vicar of Christ, and without doubt he will fulfill the will of God.

This obedience, however, is owed strictly to prelates according to the Gospel and the monastic Rule; for although mutual obedience among the brothers is good, it must never be preferred to the command of a superior. Monks are commanded to show one another obedience with discretion, and, while preserving the commands of their superiors, to anticipate one another in mutual services. And, to insert an example from our own custom: all are to be obeyed according to rank. If a brother calls on you, obey gladly; if a senior commands something, then, setting aside the command of the former, obey this one. Again, if the prior of the convent interposes his command, all mutual obedience of the brothers will cease. But if the command of the abbot intervenes, no obedience to anyone else will have force to the contrary. For he is believed to act first in the place of Christ in the monastery, and therefore he is preferred to all.

There are, moreover, seven [unclear] circumstances of the virtue of holy obedience

[unclear]: which blessed Bernard described thus. The first degree of obedience is to obey willingly: that is, to have no will of your own at all, but to believe that the good pleasure of your shepherd is wholly your own. The second is to obey simply, so that you do neither more nor otherwise than has been commanded you, nor, by doing less, omit anything. The third is to obey cheerfully, so that you show serenity in your face and sweetness in your voice. The fourth is to obey swiftly, so that the hand is not slower in the work than the command is in the voice. The fifth is to obey manfully, lest one withdraw his strength from the command and pretend that he is weak and unequal to the precepts. The sixth is to obey humbly: not proudly, not haughtily, not contentiously; for unless obedience is humble, it will bring back not reward but punishment. The seventh is to obey perseveringly, because obedience that is broken off before completion is not true obedience; and he who perseveres to the end [unclear].

But the fruit of obedience is everlasting and is never bounded by any [unclear] end. To the same degree that we obey our superiors, Christ, almighty God, obeys our prayers. Do not flatter yourself, stiff-necked monk, about persistence in prayer, for Christ does not hear in prayer the man who despises Christ's vicar in the monastery. Humility raises prayer up; obedience commends it. For obedience, as one of the fathers said, is the salvation of all the faithful, the mother of all virtues, the discoverer of the kingdom of heaven. Obedience opens the heavens, shuts the gates of hell, makes one a fellow-dweller with the angels, and has the food of all the saints. But the monk who casts off subjection to obedience, to [death?]

The fourth [degree] of humility, our father Benedict says in the Rule, is this: if, under obedience, amid hard and contrary things, or even amid any injuries inflicted, the monk embraces patience with silent conscience. This degree too takes its beginning from the third, since no one is truly to be called obedient if he has been found impatient. For, as that divine Chrysostom has it, he cannot be acceptable to the king who has been subject to the enemy; nor is he truly subject to Christ who has been enslaved to passionate and impatient flesh. For no one will be able to overcome a savage enemy unless he has learned to fight bravely against him. Patience is very necessary for us, because no virtue makes lawful progress if patience abandons it. For, [as blessed Gregory attests?], it is of greater merit to receive adversities patiently for God's sake than to toil in good works. And Saint Jerome says: He who considers that tribulation has come upon him for his sins calls forth God's mercy upon himself for doing good more fully. Therefore let the cenobite learn to set the virtue of patience against all things that befall him, if he desires to triumph over his enemies. For he conquers who suffers; he who murmurs is overcome.
