But in three things the virtue of patience is especially necessary, and is rewarded with the highest recompenses. In insults of words, the patience of a prudent man and lover of God preserves the purpose of humility; in the taking away of temporal goods and advantages it receives increase; and in bodily injury the silent conscience of virtue [unclear] the discipline. Consider now, O faithful soul, how your most beloved Savior Jesus sustained these three things most patiently for your redemption; and if you believe that you love him, do not think it burdensome, for love of him, to endure similar things with patience.

From the three steps immediately preceding we establish one consummate end of the cenobite, which, as seems reasonable to us, we call the threefold step. For by three steps, namely the second, third, and fourth, the end of the cenobitic institution is perfected, and the renunciation of one’s own will is completed. For where patience, the preserver of virtues, is joined to the renunciation of one’s own will and to obedience, every pleasure and care of the body is mortified. Whoever has deserved to ascend this threefold step has fulfilled the Lord’s commandment, which is stated in the Gospel: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” through the second step of humility, “and take up his cross” through the third, “and follow me” through the fourth.

The fifth step of humility is true confession of sins. The faithful cenobite is said to ascend into this if he confesses to his abbot, with humble trust, all evil thoughts that come into his heart, or any evils committed in secret. For if anything is committed through impatience, at the adversary’s prompting, in the preceding threefold step, it is restored in this one through contrition and humble confession. For no one is found so perfect that he does not contract the stain of earthly life, as Scripture says: “In many things we all offend.” For no one is clean from sin, not even an infant whose life upon the earth is one day. Therefore this step necessarily follows the fourth immediately; in it all the negligences of the preceding steps are corrected. True confession raises up the soldier falling in battle, heals the one wounded by the enemy, and comforts the weak and faint-hearted. Whoever, therefore, desires to stand in battle and bravely conquer the enemy should often run back to the safeguards of true confession. For it is impossible for one wounded by the enemy to recover health if he neglects to reveal the wound itself to the physician. Therefore you, faithful cenobite, who desire to save your soul and to be a good soldier of Jesus Christ, do not omit humble confession, because you will never be able to conquer the devil better than if you take care faithfully to reveal to your abbot all the thoughts and sins that he suggests to you. It is certain to me, and proved by the destruction of many, that a cenobite commits himself to being overcome by many temptations of the enemy if he refuses to keep this step.

The sixth degree of humility arises from true confession: that the monk should consider himself vile and unworthy in all things. For according to the Rule we believe him to be a true monk whom we perceive, from humble patience, to be content with every vileness and extremity in food and clothing. This vileness, however, is generally referred to ordinary things; but extremity is located in abject and more grievous hardships. For the former gladly embraces patience in meaner garments, foods, and whatever necessities of the body; the latter delights in serving the sick, the horrible, the leprous, and the abject, and in being put to shame, lowered, and despised in all things. Therefore the monk who is truly dead to the flesh and to the world should be content with every vileness and extremity; he should show himself a faithful worker in all things, and yet, because of the corruption of nature by which he offends in many things, he should believe himself vile and unworthy. Indeed, whatever good is done in this world, however holy and religiously one may live in this age, can suffice for no one to merit eternal life, unless the great mercy of God deigns to come to his aid. We receive the greatest things for the least; we await the kingdom of God not as owed to us from our merit, but as promised by grace. For the holy Apostle says: The sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us. For if we receive the justice of God without mercy, we are worthy of hell. All of us incur wrath by sinning, but we gain love by grace. No one is saved except through grace; no one is damned except through justice. Nevertheless, meanwhile, in order that we may obtain the grace of God, the zeal of our good will is required; without it grace works nothing in us toward merit. For although no one is holy by his own powers, nevertheless no one has done good well against his will. For the grace of God and the freedom of the will stand in such relation to each other that one without the other cannot suffice to save a human being, but both must necessarily come together for the performance of virtue. Since, therefore, without the grace of God we can do nothing good, we ought to judge ourselves vile and unworthy in all things, so that, while we submit ourselves to God in humility, we may always obtain greater things. And therefore this sixth degree is the merit of confession and the single foundation of all the preceding ones. For as long as the cenobite remains in this degree of humility, he will stand firm in the former ones.

The seventh degree of humility is not only to believe oneself lower than all others from the innermost affection of the heart, but also to desire with a simple mind that others believe and say this about him. This condition of holy humility is set on high, and in this time is loved by few monks. For the first condition of this deep humility seems to consist in this: that he ought to judge that he should be considered vile and abject by all. The second is that he should desire himself to be vile and abject [without?] pretense. The third condition is placed in a higher dwelling: namely, that the monk from the church

...that he may delight, with affection, to be treated most vilely and trampled upon by all. Rooted in this humility, the cenobite loves reproach and insult; he does not fear to be despised and cast aside most vilely, because, submitting himself wholly in the love of God, he places himself humbly, and hastens to insults as though to feasts, with the greatest cheerfulness. But so that you may understand the truth of this seventh degree, read the following considerations.

The first consideration directs the mind to hope in divine love, which arises from a certain pious confidence. For although a person does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred, nevertheless each person can in some measure recognize, from the disposition of his own heart, what he ought to think about his own state, good or bad.

Second, it must be considered that this good disposition of the heart and of an ordered will toward God is a sign of the love of God and of the approval of good works. For thus, when the Lord was born in the flesh, the angels sang: Peace on earth to people of good will.

Third, it should be noted that just as a good disposition of heart orders and summons the perfected mind to exercises directed toward the fear of God and the practice of virtues, so the negligence of an evil disposition inclines it especially to vices and sloth. But the consideration of this difference [unclear].

Fourth, it must be considered that an evil disposition of the heart impedes and nullifies the grace of God and merits in a person, because it makes the soul vile, base, and degenerate, and always disposes it toward graver and worst things. For indeed the root of evils of tongue and deed comes from an evil heart, as is clear in tales and many similar things.

The fifth consideration is that evil in deed and tongue is never properly examined unless first the evil of the heart is truly known. Each person, however, can examine his own heart better than others can, and consider what sort of person lies hidden within himself. Therefore for the cenobite, to whom the care of another has not been entrusted, it is enough to inspect his own heart diligently, and in no way to occupy himself in scrutinizing another's heart. But the pastor of monks, to whom the care of souls is entrusted, is also commanded to know the face of his flock.

Sixth, it should be noted from these things that it is very rash to examine another's heart, or to judge the inmost parts of brothers from words and deeds. The Lord knows those who are his, nor is it granted to a person to become a rash judge of another's heart without the rationale of office.

Seventh, it should be noted that a small evil of one's own heart, once known, would harm a person more in himself than a great evil, doubted from suspicion, concerning another's heart. For the former must be amended because it is certain and known; the latter must be piously excused because it is unknown.

Eighth, it must be considered that, since each person sees many imperfections in his own heart which he cannot recognize in others, on account of these obstacles to grace he ought to judge himself lower. Let it be granted to the [unclear] that he despise his soul as more worthless than others, even if he knows their public crimes.

[unclear] For indeed, since the root of their heart is wholly unknown to him, he cannot know how divine election was ordained concerning him from eternity. Who would believe that the thief crucified with the Lord was chosen from eternity, if he judged him according to his works? Divine election anticipates what is good; for where sin is seen to have abounded, often, by the will of divine election, greater grace is found. For divine love regards and embraces its chosen ones from eternity, and beholds them as chosen not according to the misery in which they now are, but according to their future glory. Therefore let the cenobite beware of disparaging others; let him beware of judging others, if he desires to escape eternal death. For who are you, to judge another’s servant? He stands to be judged by his own master alone.

But the disposition of this seventh degree, because of that clause “from the inmost affection of the heart,” possesses a threefold root of its origin: namely truth, hope, and charity. For indeed, when the faithful cenobite sees that he does not have his being from himself, he truly considers himself as nothing from himself; and consequently, in the same respect, he regards his works as nothing from himself, since he himself is nothing, for he knows that nothing comes to be from nothing. Therefore the monk rejoices with the truth, because in this respect he and his works are accounted as nothing, since he fears to incur the vice of falsehood if he believed himself to be something great. And therefore, withdrawing from himself, he fails, and places his being, life, and power in God alone. Secondly, this disposition arises from hope of receiving and seeking greater grace, because when a man through humility fails from himself, he approaches nearer to the grace of God. Thirdly, this disposition of humility takes its beginning from the love of God and receives continual increase in it. For whoever perfectly loves God seeks nothing in all things except his honor, nor knows how to exalt himself in anything, but desires for God’s sake to be subject to all. The more he is cast down through reproaches and injuries, the more, rejoicing, he is glad in the Lord. He rejoices that he is miserable, in order that he may proclaim the Lord glorious in himself. He who truly loves his Lord seeks nothing other than his glory.

It is clear from what we have said that the perfect charity promised to those ascending through the degrees of humility is displayed in this seventh degree. For the other five degrees that follow in the Rule add nothing to the inward perfection of the man who is in the seventh degree, but rather order the outward man, lest he dissipate the inward. Finally, from the seventh degree we could erect certain new ascents of humility, and in them raise all the other degrees higher. For a more fervent filial fear resides in him who can more fully perfect the breadth of the others.

Now that the ascents of the heart up to the degree of charity have been known, let the cenobite consider with what zeal, what effort, what perseverance he ought to exercise himself in these things, so that he may reach this seventh degree of love. to sin; and unless by repentance he recovers the holy effort, he incurs a sentence of damnation. For thus the Rule says: “But if at any time he has acted otherwise, let him know that he is to be condemned by the one whom he mocks.” For if anyone making less progress in religion is believed to be guilty before the divine judgment, what else does one who abandons the effort of making progress deserve than to receive a sentence of damnation? For where, even among those striving to make progress, an account is laid down according to the Rule concerning lesser progress, monks who despise every effort to make progress are without doubt condemned by the sentence of the judge. If therefore you do not wish to incur the danger of damnation, strive continually under the Rule to preserve the effort of one making progress.

Since we have said that the other five degrees of humility pertain to guarding the inner man, we shall also briefly set them forth.

For the monk who neglects to order his outward conduct according to the Rule will not long remain ordered in inward things. For just as a body stripped of clothing is corrupted, so humility without good conduct is emptied of force.

The eighth degree of humility, then, is set down thus in the Rule: if a monk does nothing except what the common rule of the monastery, or the examples of the elders, encourage. In this degree singularity of outward conduct contrary to the Rule is forbidden to monks; but inward singularity of greater charity and humility is forbidden to no one. Therefore let no one prefer his own inventions to the holy Rule, let no one place his own customs before the examples of the elders, because it is not enough to stand in the seventh degree if one does not keep the rule of the community.

The ninth degree of humility follows from the Rule, by which excessive talkativeness is forbidden. For it befits a monk to preserve silence, especially when he is sitting in the midst of his seniors. Indeed, one who speaks without being asked is rightly considered a fool.

The tenth degree of humility forbids readiness to laugh and levity, because whoever takes pleasure in laughter is shown to be foolish and alien to the fear of God.

The eleventh degree of humility enjoins modesty and maturity upon the monk, so that when an opportunity and permission to speak is granted, he should speak with humble gravity, without laughter and without irritation. Let the monk’s speech be rare, brief, and reasonable, because it does not befit him to say useless things who wishes to please the Most High.

The twelfth degree of humility teaches the monk to order the outward man in appearance and bearing from a humble heart, and to show by his outward conduct that he is inwardly devout. And although this degree is last in the order of all of them, nevertheless in the practice of beginners who are making progress it is first. And therefore Bernard, when describing these twelve degrees of humility, begins from this one and, ascending to the first, descends, so to speak, in order. For no one easily makes inward progress toward compunction of heart and the fear of God who does not order his conduct outwardly.

On the devout fitting of the powers for entry into the third region. Article six.

When, by the degrees of humility, the powers of the soul, especially of the interior man, have been fundamentally purified and reformed, it is now said to be very necessary in monks that they be adapted more devoutly for progress into the third region. But this diligence in striving toward higher things is necessary for the cenobite, as we have said, because where the effort to make progress is laid aside, the virtue already acquired is wholly dissipated. No one is permitted to stand still in this second region, but all are commanded to ascend to the third through continual effort. Indeed, this continual motion casts down into the first region of the flesh all the slothful and lukewarm, but sweetly, without violence, impels the humble and fervent in desire always toward the third.

Whoever, therefore, has merited from the Lord through humility to obtain the reformation of his powers is now very near to the third region of the spirit. In order that he may be able to enter it powerfully, it is necessary that, by most diligently fitting the powers of his soul, he compose them for their several operations. The intellect, however, is then said to be rightly fitted for entry into the third region when it is illumined to know the highest truth according to its capacity. The memory is composed for the same when it is fully absorbed in holding and cherishing the highest truth. But if the will is disposed to love the highest thing, which is God, for the entry [unclear]

But in order that the cenobite may be able to attain the purification of the intellectual powers, it is necessary that, dying to the world, with the mind pacified from every interior and exterior tumult, he rest, so that he may remain buried within the bosom of divine love and never withdraw from the sweetness of inward union. The mind comes to this rest by four degrees, which are rooted in a good will in four ways.

The first degree of good will lays the beginnings of the virtues; it is called an upright will. For the soul which, consenting to the law of God, subjects itself to God through an upright will, even if it still seems weak, is ordered to the path of virtue. For virtue is perfected when the flesh resists, and that the will is upright is proved by the violence done to the spirit. Yet often a will is called upright and good even when it is found to be less strong. The good that it loves it cannot always accomplish; the evil that it hates, it grieves that through weakness it has committed. Through the weakness of the flesh it is very close to the lowest region, but from the uprightness of its intention and its effort to make progress it is continually kindled toward the freedom of the spirit. For the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation depresses the sense that thinks on many things. O who could describe this battle between spirit and flesh, where the spirit itself desires to subjugate the flesh to itself through an upright will

and the weak flesh always fights against the spirit through contrary desires.

The second degree is a will strong in uprightness: so that it may both flee bravely, against the assault of the flesh, the evil that it hates, and may attain, by doing it even with toil, the good that it loves.

The third degree is a devout will, by which the mind, with enlarged heart, embraces the way of God’s commandments and delights in them as in all riches. For indeed the will does not remain strong if it has not been devout in God’s commandments.

The fourth degree is a full will, inasmuch as it in no way divides its powers, but continually extends its whole self, through the denial of all things, toward its God. For this degree three things are necessary, so that good will may be made full in us. The first is complete denial of one’s own self, because the will is proved still to be weak if it is not mortified through every kind of self-denial. The second thing required for full good will is called perfect resignation; if anyone desires to grasp it, let him fervently ascend the third degree of humility. The third member necessary for the fourth degree of good will is called the total extension of the will into God; through this the soul, admitted into divine love and sweetly burning, is in a certain way transformed into the same, and is frequently admitted into the third region.

Finally, according to Bernard’s judgment, that transformation into divine love is love, affection, adherence, union, charity, or fruition; no one can reach it unless he has learned to mortify all his affections in the fervor of the spirit. For the spirit of a man who has his heart raised upward into God is called perfect will, and is united with God by a most sweet bond. In these degrees of good will, therefore, the faithful cenobite ought without interruption to direct his effort upward, and always to examine with prudent care how much he is advancing or falling back. For Saint Bernard says: Just as he who remains in a vicious will is contemptible, so he who does not strive to advance in the others is blameworthy. For where the effort to advance is laid aside, the danger of falling back is incurred.

On the exemplary and experiential certainty of all the foregoing.

Article VII.

Although a man does not know whether he is worthy of love or [hatred?], nevertheless each person can, by diligently examining his conscience, recognize what he ought to think about the condition of his state. The testimony of his own conscience reveals what sort each person is inwardly, hidden within himself. Therefore, so that the cenobite may clearly discern the condition of his state, he ought, according to John Castellensis on the Rule, to observe three things in his conscience, without which a good Chris-

is made a Christian: no one is judged a good man or monk.

First, therefore, what is required for a good man is the testimony of a good conscience: namely, that no mortal sin lies hidden in the conscience. For a mind that is polluted by the guilt of mortal sin testifies that the state of the conscience is evil. Therefore each monk must examine himself diligently and carefully cleanse himself of the faults he has committed, according to the ordinance of the Church. But whoever, on examining his conscience, finds it clean from mortal sin should offer humble praises to God and should not omit to add the examination of the following matters.

The second thing necessary for a good man is to aim chiefly at God in all works and, as far as he can, to order all things to his praise and honor. But if, because the multitude and variety of works impede him, a man cannot always actually keep God before his eyes, at least habitually let him conform his intention of living according to the most pleasing will of God to this desire.

The third is that in all things he obey God and holy mother Church and the prelates set over him, and not withdraw from the path of right and enlightened reason; for whoever despises this threefold obedience has denied the faith. It is therefore necessary that obedience be shown equally to these three in right order, according to the ordinance of reason, so that the life of the monk may remain blameless in its actions, without fear.

These three things, possessed with humble sincerity, make a good man and show the state of a conscience hoping well in the Lord. But the man to whom one of these is lacking is not perfectly good, even if he seems to be good. But if, repentant of his sins, he has resolved henceforth to fulfill these three things, he is now made good and pleasing to God, however evil he may have been considered before. Furthermore, in order that from a good man a good religious, or spiritual man, may be born, according to the aforesaid [unclear], three other things are required.

The first thing required for making a good religious is that purity of heart be cleansed, through zeal for discipline, from every defilement or incitement of the flesh. This purity is never better acquired than if the world, with all its things, is despised.

The second thing by which a good man is made a good religious is called spiritual freedom in God. This, once the images of all things have been excluded, can raise itself upward to God, unencumbered in all exercises, and continually lift itself up without impediment in thanksgiving with devout prayers.

In the third way a good man is made spiritually good when, through love, the desire of the spirit is united with God by fixed degrees. These last two things make our cenobite spiritual and often introduce him to the citizens of the third region. Therefore whoever desires to trust rightly in the testimony of his conscience should humbly strive to exercise himself in the aforesaid things, because security is never prudently presumed when danger is not avoided. to live in negligences and sins, and to be unwilling to amend the errors committed? The confidence of the righteous, arising from the testimony of a good conscience, is the best hope, and is continually subject to God in humble service. But the impious and sinners, disturbed by their own actions, raise themselves up against God; they do not trust in the testimony of conscience, but rather presume vainly.

There follow the seven roots of divine fear, which are laid as foundations in the first degree of humility.

Since this second region chiefly instructs the cenobite, in order, through the degrees of humility proceeding from the fear of God, it is necessary for him to recognize clearly the roots of that fear, if he wishes by ascending to arrive at the love of God. Therefore, so that we may be able to construct this spiritual house to perfection, we must place those roots in order in the foundation. We have not set them out in the first degree of humility for this reason: lest we confuse the order of the things to be said by excessive length. There are, then, seven roots of the fear of God, by which the cenobite is led to compunction and, advancing in true humility, is more strongly rooted.

The first root of the fear and love of God is intent meditation on the incomprehensible divine majesty: God is comprehended the less, the more curiously he is investigated by man. For the prophet says: Truly you are a hidden God. This meditation begets wonder at divine perfection; wonder causes reverence; from reverence arises fear of majesty; and from fear worship is produced. Meditation upon the supreme goodness is divided, according to our capacity, into seven considerations, which are not unsuitably adapted to the seven days of the week, or even to the seven canonical hours. And although that highest and most perfect goodness is abundantly sufficient for us as material for meditation, yet because it belongs to few to be able to ascend to invisible things without visible things, we wish through known things to raise the minds of the weak to things unknown. For the holy apostle says: The invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are perceived, being understood through the things that have been made; his everlasting power also and divinity, so that they are without excuse.

First, therefore, the wondrous power of God's might is worthy of praise in the principal work of creation, since he was able to bring forth all things from nothing, and by his will alone created things so great, so solid, so varied, and noble. From this consideration wonder at divine might arises, through which a person is summoned to the fear of God.

Secondly, the provident wisdom of God is worthy of praise, because, knowing all things,

[unclear]; and all things that he has created he governs by his providence. He knows all things, understands all things, disposes all things by his counsel, encloses all things by his command. For, as a certain lover of the wisdom of the world said: God is a sphere whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere. He is within all things and is not enclosed; he is outside all things and is not excluded; he is beneath all things and is not oppressed; he is above all things and is not borne up. He himself contains all things, who, though wholly everywhere, is enclosed in no place; great and immeasurable, he is bounded by no quantity. He orders all things as he wills; stable in himself always and immovable, he changes the vicissitudes of things; for the good he mercifully prepares eternal rewards without passion of mind; angry without disturbance, he condemns the unjust. Great without magnitude, immeasurable without quantity, he has set a limit to things; governing the world, he disposes all things.

Third, the merciful kindness of God is praiseworthy in our redemption, because the man whom he created in his own image, fallen so miserably into the pit of damnation, he restored so mercifully. O what shall I, a little worm, indeed nothing in comparison with my maker, render to the supreme and incomprehensible majesty, who, when I did not exist, created me by his own power; when I had perished, became man for my sake and, dying on the cross, redeemed me? What shall I repay you, mediator of God and men, Jesus, savior of the world, who, though you are God most high and inestimable, became man for me, most vile, and willed to undergo things so vile and unworthy? Behold, my heart speaks to you; all my inward parts incline toward you, since no voice can express what you give your faithful to feel within, in the heart, concerning your most innocent passion.

Fourth, in the work of our justification the kindly patience of God is praiseworthy, because he not only mercifully tolerates sinners but also calls them, to be justified, to repentance with promises of eternal joys. Who could suffice to praise this kindness of the most indulgent Father, who so mercifully justifies sinners returning to him, grants after a fall the grace of meriting, orders manifold opportunities for living well, and supplies his sacraments to the penitent as certain vessels of grace? Finally, for compunction, instruction, consolation, and thanksgiving, he pours the Holy Spirit into his faithful, making friends and sons out of enemies. He does not consider what sort of sinner a person previously was; he seeks only that henceforth he remain faithful to him. Great is the kindness of divine compassion, which so mercifully receives the penitent to pardon, and even promises them great rewards after guilt.

Fifth, the profound justice of God is praiseworthy in the damnation of the reprobate, because he allows no evil to pass unpunished, depriving the sinner of the good which the fool is not afraid to lose by sinning. Finally, to speak in our manner, the supreme purity of God is shown praiseworthy in this: that every sin and

[unclear], he abominates as though a putrid corpse. We have also recognized that his wisdom is praiseworthy in the damnation of the impious, because, drawing God’s goods out of evils, he compels them to serve him in punishment, who, sinning against justice, were unwilling to be subject in guilt.

Sixth, the generous munificence of God is praiseworthy in the glorification of the blessed, because for a small merit he rewards his elect with so ineffable a recompense, as though he gives immortal gifts together with the holy angels.

Seventh, the incomprehensible excellence of God is praiseworthy in itself, because he orders [unclear] according to his providence and, most tranquil in himself, always remains immovable, without motion or time. The contemplation of this seventh consideration belongs to the sabbath of eternal happiness, in which there is now no work of laborious activity, but the blessedness of a happy eternal dwelling and rest. For just as God, the creator of all things, is read to have completed all his work and rested on the seventh day, so not work but eternal rest will be laid upon the righteous in the heavenly sabbath. Therefore, if we desire happily to arrive at those heavenly mansions, let us rest in God alone, in whom the rational creature is perfected by resting; having been perfected through the adherence of love, it rejoices with the Lord in ineffable union and joy. Henceforth, for praising God, let pure devotion seek nothing outside God, because God himself, almighty, perfect, and most wise, suffices for all as the material of his own praise, and exceeds all praise by his infinite perfections. For Scripture says: Praise the Lord as much as you can; he will still surpass it. For he is greater than all praise, and therefore he is to be praised by us most humbly in himself and for himself rather than from creatures.

From the aforesaid considerations concerning God, a manifold and varied affection of devotion arises; through it also a worthier effect of prayer is generated according to the desire of the affection. For when meditation of the heart is taken up concerning the majesty or power of God, reverent admiration is produced. But when we begin to meditate on his inexpressible wisdom, confounded by our foolish imperfection, we accuse ourselves. Thus consequently, from consideration of the mercy of God, hope of pardon is received; from his patience, love of the heart is generated; from justice, humiliation is born; from meditation on munificence, gratitude. For just as fire, once kindled, increases in magnitude according to the quality of the wood, so according to various meditations on God the ardor of devotion rises up in prayers among those who love God.

On meditation on the work of our redemption. Root II.

The second root of the fear and love of God is placed in meditation on our redemption, which, in the life, conduct, doctrine, and passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, through exercises

[unclear] is generated. Among all meditations we believe this one to be more useful for us, in which we know our salvation and the sum of eternal happiness to be contained. And note that the Passion of the Lord, with respect to its procedure, was unjust; with respect to its manner, shameful; with respect to its pain, bitter; and with respect to its effect, fruitful; and therefore it is always to be held in memory.

First, with respect to its procedure, it was unjust, because, born of a virgin, he neither contracted sin nor committed it, nor was deceit found in his mouth. For death is inflicted on us for sin; but he could not justly die who was always righteous and innocent, without any sin. Finally, he was killed contrary to human law, if sentence of death is passed upon a man neither confessed nor convicted of a crime. The Savior was accused before Pilate on three charges: that, calling himself a king, he forbade tribute to Caesar; third, that he made himself the Son of God. The Gospel speaks of the first two, and the accusation is shown to be false. For concerning the first, the contrary was plainly established, since Christ said that his kingdom was not earthly. The falsity of the second likewise did not escape Pilate, who knew that Jesus had commanded that the things which were Caesar's should be given to Caesar. When questioned by the governor about the third, he was silent, because Pilate was unworthy to hear of Jesus' divine generation or even his human birth. His Passion also took place contrary to custom, because it received no delay of time. He is not put in prison according to custom; nothing is deliberated in his case; but, once seized, he is immediately dragged to the judge to be subjected to death; scourged, spat upon, and afflicted with many wrongs, blows, and mockeries, he is nailed to the cross. Third, it was contrary to the law of nature, and procured from obstinate hatred of heart. For nature forbids raging against the dead, and shudders at tearing with new wounds a body that has been killed. For our Redeemer, dead on the cross, is pierced with a lance, and, contrary to the law of nature, the deceased is wounded by the impious.

Second, the Passion of Christ, with respect to its manner, is said to have been shameful for the six causes that follow. First, because of the paltry price, since blood of incomparable value is sold by a disciple for thirty pieces of silver, for which no one would deign to sell his little ass. Second, because of the shameful office, for, full of wounds and half-dead, he is compelled to carry his own cross, which is found to have been done to no robber. Third, because of the indignity of the place, since he is crucified outside the city in the place of Calvary, where robbers and wicked murderers are punished for their deserts. Fourth, because of the shameful punishment, since he is hung naked on the cross, which penalty is owed only to robbers and wicked men. Indeed, as Scripture says, the Redeemer of the world was condemned to a most shameful death. Fifth, because of the shameful mockery, since he is hung naked on the cross before the whole multitude, and is blasphemed by all as if foolish and senseless. Of this the psalmist says: All day long my shame is before me. Sixth, because of the shameful company, for, counted with the wicked, he is hung in the midst of robbers. What are you doing now, O Christian soul? Behold, your Savior is hung in the middle between robbers, and you do not fear to sit in the first place in the council?

Third, the most holy Passion of Christ was most bitter with respect to its pain, for seven reasons. First, because of the delicate liveliness of his flesh, which in natural complexion was the best, and therefore was more grievously afflicted in the suffering of pain. For delicate flesh hurts more than flesh coarse by natural condition. Therefore, since the flesh of Christ was subtle and delicate, it emitted a bloody sweat in the garden. Second, because of the quality of those killing him, for Christ was not killed by foreigners, but by his own proper kinsmen and neighbors, just as he had earlier complained through the prophet: My people, what have I done to you? For one suffers more tolerably from foreigners and enemies than from one's own, for whom at least friends, from nearness of blood, have compassion. Third, because of the bitterness of the Passion, since he is afflicted more in those places in which pain is felt more because of the nerves. For, raised up on the cross, he is fastened through hands and feet; thirsting, the Lord of all is given gall and hyssop to drink. For the psalmist says of him: They dug through my hands and my feet; they numbered all my bones. Who could conceive in his mind the pain of your most holy heart, O good Jesus, when the very hard nails began so cruelly to pierce your hands and feet? Would that my soul may always show itself grateful to you; would that the recollection of your most holy Passion may not depart from my memory. Easily shall I be able to obtain from you the effect of my prayers, if it happens that I delight without interruption in the exercise of your Passion. Let each person think what he can; I prefer the memory of your Passion to all exercises, through which I trust that I shall receive in prayers whatever accords with salvation. Fourth

[Fifth?], because of its long duration, the passion of Christ was singular. For he suffers in reputation, because, falsely accused by the impious, he is blasphemed.

He suffered also in his possessions, because, naked and stripped, he was hung upon the wood, and his garments are divided by lot among the soldiers. He suffers in his soul, because, forefeeling the bitterness of the passion, he was sorrowful even unto death. He suffered in his whole body, since from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there was no soundness in him.

He suffers in his friends, since he is betrayed by a disciple, deserted by all, and even publicly denied by Peter. He is afflicted also in the compassion of his mother, whose most holy soul the sword of sorrow is recorded to have pierced. He suffered from the ingratitude of many, because he foreknew that the death which he bore in suffering for all would be lost in so many of the reprobate. Finally, he suffered in all his senses, as we are taught from the Gospel. He suffers in his eyes, because after many tears had been shed they are covered with a cloth. He suffers in his hearing, when amid many insults and outrages he is mocked and blasphemed. He suffers in his smell, since he is defiled by the foul spittle of the Jews. He suffers in touch, because, thirsting, he is given gall and vinegar to drink. Sixth, because of the cause of the passion, which was solely the envy of the Jews, although he was plainly without any fault. For truly, whoever suffers unjustly is tormented all the more in his spirit. But the innocent Son of God dies for our sins; he is tormented for our crimes, as is read in Isaiah: Truly he himself bore our infirmities. Seventh, because of the lack of all consolation, since Christ found no one consoling him in his passion. For he says in the Psalm: You have put friend and neighbor far from me. Indeed, his acquaintances stood far off.

Fourth, how fruitful the passion of Christ was; this is chiefly to be considered in three things. First, the remission of sins was accomplished; second, the bestowal of grace; third, the display of glory. And these three things are indicated by the title fixed to the cross, which, as the evangelist says, contained the cause of Jesus’ passion: Jesus of Nazareth, king of the Jews. Jesus, saving sinners, with respect to the first; Nazarene, bestowing the flower of grace, with respect to the second; king of the Jews, showing the heavenly kingdom to those who confess him, with respect to the third.

Moreover, in this second root we have arranged meditations on the passion of the Lord for the several hours of the seven days of the week. We have therefore placed them after the end of the third region, lest at this point, by their excessive length, we disturb the order of the things to be said. For what we have now set forth we see to pertain rather to reading than to meditation, and therefore we postpone them.

On the Meditation of the Benefits of God. Root II.

The third root of divine fear and love is fixed in meditations on the benefits of God, through which one comes to the grace of devotion. For truly, the beginning of devotion is placed in meditation on the benefits of God, from the memory of which love is generated. But the middle, insofar as progress in that very meditation desires nothing other than to please God above all things,

by which he knows that without any merit of his own he has been forestalled with many benefits. Hence he loves God above all things with burning desire and with the pure fervor of the mind, and longs to cleave continually to him alone, without intermediary. And although the merciful God has bestowed many things specially upon each one of us, nevertheless, because we write these our tokens not for one but for many, we must briefly bring forward not particular benefits assigned to individuals, but general benefits set before all. Therefore we include the more important ones under the number seven, so that through the seven days of the week, or even in the canonical hours themselves, we may have ready at hand material for daily meditation. But if anyone already dwells in higher things through the elevation of the mind toward God, let him not require these things, proposed as they are for novices. But he who, because of the weakness of his mind, cannot ascend to that supreme summit of contemplation, should strive to exercise himself more fervently in these meditations on the benefits of God, so that, while he diligently continues in the lower things, he may, purified and stronger, ascend to the higher. Let the devout monk therefore remember what he has received from the Lord God, so that he may be able to show himself grateful. Let him render to God what he has received, if he is good [unclear] he desires [unclear]. with his ornaments, and those whom he created intellectual beings in his own image he also mercifully called to the heavenly kingdoms. What more could he have given us, who, when we did not exist, created us and gave us himself? But what can we render to our Creator, we who by our own merit are sinners and weak? Let us render what we are; let us render what we owe: namely, faithful service for the body which we have received from the Lord, and sincere love for the soul by which we were created in the image of God. For thus the prophet admonishes us in the psalm: Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling. Serve faithfully; love reverently. On the part of the body, offer faithful service to your Creator, and on the part of the soul love him with all your strength. Serve him because he is powerful and a great Lord; love him because he is good. His power is shown in your creation; his goodness is declared in your restoration. Since he created you by his power when you did not exist, he deserves faithful service; since he restored you when you had fallen by his goodness, he deserves the affection of sincere love. For truly he is our Father through love; he is Lord through incomprehensible power.

Secondly, he gave us faith with the sacraments, since, just as he created us without our will, so without our merit he called us to the faith. For Christ says to his disciples in the holy Gospel: You did not choose me; rather, I chose you. Through faith the Christian soul is led back to its principle; through the sacraments it is renewed. Therefore, incorporated into Christ through the faith and the sacraments which he gave, we are bound to offer perpetual adherence, and to remain continually in his holy covenant. we have renounced his pomps; we have promised that we shall cleave perpetually to Christ, those who lifted us from the sacred font standing as sureties for us before the Lord in the faith of our parents. Let us therefore always say from the heart with the prophet: “It is good for me to cleave to God, to place my hope in the Lord God.”

Third, almighty God gave us the craft of uprightness and the teachings of truth. For these we are bound to our creator in faithful execution and perpetual service without deceit. We are therefore commanded above all to do all things to the praise of God, and in everything that we do chiefly to raise our intention toward his honor. For only a good intention directed toward God distinguishes works; love alone makes them fruitful. Behold, the Lord bestowed upon us the craft of nature for praising him; he gave, besides, the teachings of salvation through the law; he requires from us praise and love above all things. Let us therefore exercise, to the honor of God, the craft bestowed upon us, and let the pure eye of intention be formed through the teaching of the law.

Fourth, the merciful Father bestowed upon us the world with its necessary elements; for these he requires from us due and sincere contemplation of himself. Whatever we discern in this world ought to lead us to the memory of God and continually stir us to love its creator above all things. Hence Bernard, [unclear] in sacred matters, says: “The whole and true lover of God, wherever he turns, has before him a familiar reminder of his creator, and uses things as a mirror, and in such thinking is raised up from the creature to the creator. For concerning each thing he says: If those things seem good, beautiful, and sweet which, having been created, change and pass away with time, what goodness, beauty, and sweetness has God, their author, who remains forever, who has reserved for himself things incomparably better than these?” By this consideration of things the devout man looks upon all human beings with the simple eye of the mind, as if upon the likeness of the image of God, and does not curiously attend in them to the body’s appearance, pleasing or displeasing. For in a human being he considers not what he sees outwardly, but the image of the creator, which he knows to be a sharer in eternal happiness.

Fifth, the Son of God offered himself in torments for us, and redeemed us, lost as we were, from the ruin of everlasting death by his blood. We are commanded to render to this love of our savior a willing imitation, if we desire to arrive at his kingdom. For the prince of the apostles says to the faithful: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow in his footsteps.” What shall I render to you, O good Jesus, for your benefits toward me, so great and so immeasurable? I shall suffer with you in heart, I shall suffer with you in deed; I shall imitate you in the affections of the mind according to my ability.

[unclear] of salvation so negligently and without fruit of merits, when we have nothing more precious than time? Behold, now, in a brief span of time, we can earn the joys of eternal happiness; and we all neglect to do what is good. Woe to us, foolish and mad, who have received nothing in this world more precious than time, and yet are accustomed to expend nothing more cheaply. For now an acceptable time is granted to us; now the days of salvation are bestowed, in which we ought to apply ourselves to holy works with the greatest fervor, and always foresee the hour of death.

Seventh, God has set before us heaven filled with all joys, and has promised himself, with all things contained in it, as a reward. For this munificence of our Savior we ought to apply ourselves to holy works of mercy, and to show ourselves, as far as we can, imitators of God. To this the Lord exhorts us in the holy Gospels: Be merciful, as your Father God also is merciful. Likewise at the end of the world, when the day of judgment has come, the merciful, as the Lord himself promises, will go into eternal life, since he who has shown mercy will obtain mercy. And lest any of the monks say to me, “I can expend mercy on no one, since religion permits me to possess nothing at all,” let us know that among the necessary works of mercy, spiritual works are the more excellent. If you, a monk, wish to be merciful, pray to God for the wretched; bestow saving doctrine on the unlearned.

Therefore the sum of meditation on God’s benefits rests upon three exercises, in which it is principally wholly contained. In the first, indeed, we ought to attribute all things to God, not to ourselves; in the second, by remembering God’s benefits, to exercise ourselves in zeal for love; in the third, always to give thanks from a pure heart for the benefits received. But if by these exercises concerning benefits we wish our heart to grow toward the love of God, we ought to consider six conditions in the gifts of the Lord themselves. First, consider that the gift of God is thoroughly noble; second, how especially fruitful and useful it is to you; third, because it is varied, manifold, and very frequently repeated. And these three consider the gift as ordered in itself; the two that follow regard the person of the giver; the last notes the condition of the recipient. Fourth, therefore, consider the great affection of the giver toward you; fifth, his inestimable dignity; sixth, that you, receiving great things from the Greatest, are vile and contemptible, and unworthy of all things. From these considerations of benefits the love of God is accustomed to arise in the mind of a devout person, and, advancing by certain steps, to lift the spirit to contemplation.

[unclear] has done, we bring back to mind by considering; and we shall know how unworthy, vile, and altogether undeserving we are in all things. But four things ought to lead a man to knowledge of himself; from the consideration of these it is most fitting that we should love God.

First, therefore, let the faithful man consider the beginning of his own creation, and he will find that, when he did not exist, he was created from the goodness of God alone. Who could have asked God, when no one existed? That highest and utterly ineffable Good created you in his own image, O man, when you did not exist; from goodness alone he made you a sharer in his goodness. What did you deserve? Or what advantage could your creation bring to almighty God, who, always subsisting unchangeable in himself, admits no accident? Nothing is new to God; nothing can be old to the highest and unchangeable Good. He is always what he can be, for neither does the best become better, nor the greatest become greater. God created you by his goodness, not because your creation was necessary to him, but because it was advantageous to you alone. Whoever, by continual meditation, considers this goodness of God deservedly praises his Creator.

Secondly, lest you be lifted up into pride, O man, consider the vileness of your creation: how you were made from the mud of the earth, and after a little while, consumed by worms, you will return into the earth as dust. Why then are you proud, earth and ashes? Your conception contains guilt, your birth misery, your life punishment, the dissolution of death anguish. For a man born of woman lives a short time, is filled with many miseries, and then is most miserable when, miserable as he is in the flesh, he does not recognize himself.

Thirdly, consider the origin of your conception, and you will find your soul defiled by the foulness of original sin. For we are born children of wrath, but, receiving the grace of baptism in the blood of Christ Jesus, we are cleansed from the original stain. Deservedly, through this consideration, we love our Savior, by whose mercy we have been cleansed from the original stain.

Fourthly, faithful soul, consider how exceedingly vile you have made yourself by repeating your ways in the act of sin: how you have shown yourself an adulteress to Christ your spouse, when he had joined you to himself through his blood, wholly unstained. What are you doing, O wretched one? Why do you desert your most loving spouse, or why, foolish one, do you withdraw from your beginning? Know yourself to be placed in the flesh, not so that you may consent to its vices and concupiscences, but rather so that you may resist by the command of reason. For as often as you have, by dissembling, so to speak, surrendered your consent to the disordered motions of the flesh and those contrary to divine rectitude, so often, turned away from the highest Good and from your spouse, you show yourself an adulteress. Beware, beware, O soul redeemed by the blood of Christ, lest the love of the flesh deceive you; for just as the first man, deceived by love of his woman companion, fell into death, so every soul that consents to the pleasures of its flesh shamefully withdraws from its beginning, which is God. But alas, wretched one, where have you fallen? You have dwelt in

You have forsaken the fountain of wisdom; you have been turned backward; you have committed adultery. But hear my counsel, and return [as quickly as possible?] to Jesus, the guide of your youth; submit yourself wholly to him in humility. He is merciful. When you return to him, he will gladly receive you; he will forgive your faults, and, if you ask, he will bestow the grace of his love. But you must withdraw from the affections of your flesh if you desire to come into the sight of your Savior. Therefore, if you turn to Jesus, turn in truth, because you cannot love anything except the true highest truth.

There is also another mode of self-knowledge, which is taken up with respect to God, whenever the incomparable comparison between God and man is considered. On this mode Bernard, illustrious in contemplation, says: Never does the measure of human imperfection perceive itself better than in the light of the face of God and in the mirror of divine vision. For there, the more one is in the day and the more one sees what is lacking in oneself, the more one amends day by day whatever has strayed into unlikeness, and approaches, by likeness, him from whom one has been far removed by unlikeness. Let us therefore raise a suppliant mind to the mirror of divine perfection; let us submit our affection to that immutable good, so that in the wisdom of God we may be able to perceive our foolishness, and in his power to consider our weakness.

On Keeping the Memory of One’s Sins.

The root of living fear of God is the memory of sins and the very foulness of sin when pondered. For indeed, the person who truly understands the shamefulness of mortal sin is always terrified of the pit of this evil. In order that we may in some way recognize the gravity of sin, you must consider the seven things that follow.

First, then, consider the beauty of God’s justice, to which sin is wholly contrary and therefore most of all to be fled. For through sin the soul is utterly turned away from the highest good, and the love that is naturally in it toward its principle is changed into hatred. For just as all good things come from the first good, so every love, toward whatever good it is borne, is naturally kindled by that same source. For since our love cannot rest in any goods as in its end, it has, as the end where it is to be stilled, the same good that it had also as its beginning. Therefore, whenever sin is committed against the beauty of God’s justice, the soul is separated from its own principle. For since God is charity, he requires love in the soul; since he is peace, he requires peace; since he loves likeness, he hates unlikeness.

Second, consider the enormity of sin, and ponder diligently how much its foulness displeases God. Behold, because of pride, the just God cast the most noble angel Lucifer out of heaven, and with his accomplices condemned him to the burning of eternal fire. Likewise our first parents

Magnus est cui peccasti et immensus: terribilis et gloriosus: cuiꝰ maie¬</p>

[unclear] compelled Adam and Eve to leave paradise because of disobedience, and by a just judgment condemned the whole human race, in their crime, under a twofold sentence of death. Finally, let us review the whole history of the Old and New Testament, and we shall find that what was known to have been rashly committed against the justice of God was often severely punished. The gravity of the crime is therefore easily recognized if the strictness of the vengeance that followed is considered.

Third, consider how grave a scandal arises from sin, especially when one sins before others. For he who by his own evil example provokes someone to sin shows himself to be an adversary of God. For God, of his mercy, resolved by his own will to save souls redeemed by the blood of his only-begotten Son; this man, through evil example, desires to destroy them through aversion from God. The sin of scandal, with respect to guilt, is for this reason called very grave, because, as we have said, it is opposed to God. But if one who gives occasion for harm is to be thought to have done the harm, the sinner subjects himself to condemnation by as many sentences of death as the people whom by his own evil example he made fall into mortal crime. For Christ says in the holy Gospel: Woe to the man through whom scandal comes. And again he says: Whoever scandalizes one of these little ones believing in me, it is expedient for him that a millstone turned by a donkey be hung around his neck and that he be sunk in the depth of the sea. True repentance is rare in one who scandalizes little ones, because, when he neglects to restore another’s loss, he by no means attains the fruit of saving penitence.

Fourth, consider the negligence of your ungrateful heart: since you, created in the image of God, ought to have loved your maker above all things, yet by your sins you dishonor him in many ways. You ought to devote continual service of love to Christ the Son of God, by whose blood you have been redeemed; but you do not fear to love the flesh more than Jesus your savior. Finally, with a compassionate mind you ought daily to turn over in your mind his most holy Passion; and you are accustomed to think of nothing less than that. Adopted among the sons of God by mercy alone, you ought by imitation to show yourself worthy of the heavenly calling; and still you do not dread to lie in the lowest things through sloth. And why do I say many things? Behold, you who are marked with the Holy Spirit are reckoned with the angels; you are called to the inheritance of the sons of God; you are invited by all the saints to the feasts of paradise; you daily partake of the body and blood of our savior Jesus Christ; and nevertheless you do not observe the commandments of God and of the Rule which you promised, that you might be blessed. Examine your conscience diligently, therefore, and you will find that you ought to do many good things which you omit, and to omit many more evil things which you commit against God’s good pleasure.

Fifth, consider whom you offend by sinning: for it is not a man but God, not a creature but the creator. Great is he against whom you have sinned, and immeasurable; terrible and glorious; whose majes-

[At whose majesty?] the angels tremble; at whose might all the powers of heaven marvel. To the highest and immutable good, God, the beginning and end of every creature, the rational spirit ought to devote love and the desire for a cleaving that is beyond human understanding; and, despising all phantasms, it ought to raise itself higher, wholly, to that which is truly one, as to its own center. It can lift itself toward this the more easily, the more, leaving all other things, it has striven to unite itself to itself. For by the power of that One itself union comes about everywhere; nor are like things more easily united with one another for any other reason than that in quality they are one. Therefore the mind is then most rightly said to be united with the One itself, the principle of things, when it itself, having especially been made one in itself, separated from every multitude, and above all imagination, reason, and understanding, escapes as its own unity alone, enjoying through loving affection the unity of God, joining, so to speak, its own center with the center of the universe. But when the human mind itself, ill at ease in its quasi-marriage with the flesh, is turned toward any animal passions whatever, then that unity itself is badly changed into a multitude contrary to the sole One, and it becomes the more removed from its principle, the more it has been divided from itself. Finally the mind itself contracts great difficulty in returning to that ineffable divine One whenever, confused in itself, it falls into the sin of apostasy. Think now how great and ineffable is he against whose honor sin is committed; and since you cannot understand the greatness of his majesty, learn humbly to fear his power.

Sixth, consider what, wretched one, you have lost by sinning, so that, when the magnitude of the loss is known, repentance may hasten and restore through tears what was lost. What then, wretched one, have you lost by sinning? Hear what you have lost. You had been made a son of God by grace, a companion of angels, a member of Christ, and chosen as heir of eternal happiness; you ought to have lived and rejoiced without end in the good things of the Lord with all the saints. But what became of you when you sinned? You were compared to foolish beasts and made like them. For when you were in honor, you refused to understand; you abandoned the fountain of life; by sinning you were made a companion and member of the devil, a harlot of Antichrist, an heir of hell. You abandoned life; you chose everlasting death. If you fear the sentence, change your will, and you will find forgiveness.

Seventh, consider what you have deserved by sinning; for if eternal death is inflicted for one sin, think what one who has committed many, not to say innumerable, deserves. For the soul that has sinned shall itself die. Moreover, even through one mortal sin you have deserved to become a companion of the devil, to be deprived of all the joys of heaven, to be burned forever in the fires of hell. These are the rewards that sin has brought you; these are the gifts it promised.

Now therefore, from these seven considerations, make a plaster for the [soul?].

wound me: take up for yourself the goad of compunction, so that you may reach the root of fear. But hurry, and do not put it off from day to day, since he who receives penitents with humble confession has not promised tomorrow to the one who delays. For where haste finds pardon, delay often cuts off life. The hope of a longer life drags many to destruction, because, while they trust that they can live longer in this world, they make the time for penitence pass by without penitence. But you, man, if you accept my counsel, do not put off penitence, since you are utterly ignorant of what tomorrow will bring you. For he deserves to lose the time for penitence who so often is not afraid to postpone the zeal for repenting.

On the Vanity of Present Things and the Eternity of Future Things

[unclear]: if the vanity of visible things and the eternity of invisible things are pondered with diligent attention. For the things that we perceive in this world are wholly subject to vanity and corruption, and indeed will endure for a very brief time. All mortal things hang under an uncertain chance, and by their own mutability promise flight. Whatever you have today will perhaps leave you tomorrow; or while you are speaking it will cease to be yours. For we perceive nothing in this world as lasting and stable, but see all things changing with time.

Therefore ascend the [unclear] watchtower of your mind, O faithful cenobite, and consider that all things which time contains are nothing, since whatever is now seen as visible will shortly be corrupted. Take from past things a consideration of present things, and see that what has passed away does not exist, and what now seems to exist will shortly not exist. Where are the kings of the nations, where the princes, where the leaders, where the men once powerful in the world? Where are all the lovers of the world, where the men who despised the arduous way of heaven? Finally, where are all those once known to you in the world, whom death has meanwhile snatched away while you were in the cloister? Behold, from the beginning of the world, both those who lived for many times and those who lived for few have all died in their own generation, and according to the diversity of their merits they have also received different rewards, with justice dictating. The lovers of God receive bright everlasting dwellings, filled with inestimable joys, associated with the Creator of all things; and the worshippers of the world, scorning God’s commandments, once swollen here with honors, puffed up with knowledge, immersed in riches, given over to pleasures and vices, have descended to hell to be tormented without end. What, I ask, does the once laborious contempt of the world, contrary to the flesh, now harm the saints in heaven, for which they have eternal [unclear], compared with the consolation of the flesh once enjoyed, for which they now receive the torments of eternal damnation? Again, descending more deeply, with the gaze of the mind [if opportunity is present], try, as far as you can, to fix yourself in the abyss of infinite depth, and to consider how long that which is eternal is. Eternal is the time which is closed by no end, bounded by no space. The saints of God will exult forever in blessed glory. Sinners in hell will burn in misery. O eternal name, terrible without end: who will be able to think of you or speak of you without fear? Truly, he who thinks of you never sins forever. The eternal has no end. Hear a comparison; and since it will not be sufficient for eternity, receive fear. If a heap of sand were set up in the size of Mount Olympus, stretched up to heaven, from which, after ten thousand years ten times over, a little bird were to consume only one grain, that mountain would by no means be said to be destined to last forever, but would be subject to an end; and although after innumerable years, nevertheless sometime it would cease. Yet all that time during which something of the mountain remained, however very long it might be, would nevertheless, in comparison, seem nothing beside eternity. That which is eternal admits neither an imagining of an end, nor hope of completion, nor any boundary.

O therefore how foolish, how mad is the man who casts away this consideration of eternity, and uselessly spends the acceptable time granted to him for earning eternal goods. The hour will come, and now hastens near, in which the wretch, when he is no longer able to do better, will learn what the eternal is. But you, my monk, who desire to be faithful, cast away from yourself all concern for the world; set all your care upon the love of God. Do nothing, think nothing, except what can lead you to the love of your Creator, or what you know pertains to the edification of others or to pure bodily necessity. Separate, I pray, from the lowest things, so that you may be able to delight in eternal goods. Let no solicitude of the flesh remove you from the inward tranquility of the mind; let no pleasure corrupt you. Strive always to persist in prayers with devotion as much as you are able, and more often to raise yourself upward through the affection of love.

On Always Having Zeal for God.

The seventh root of the fear of God is zeal for God, in which the monk is commanded to exercise himself not a little. For no one tolerates calmly the injuries of his lord if he truly loves him. Therefore you, monk, who desire to be a faithful servant of Jesus Christ, do not neglect his zeal in yourself; when you see an injury to God, do not pretend not to notice it, because whoever does not at once resist those who disparage him is proved to love his Lord less. Let men know you as such a lover of God and enemy of vices that in your presence they do not dare to speak evil, nor to do anything evil while you look on [unclear].

...and let them not presume [unclear]. Be conspicuous for uprightness of mind, renowned for the merit of your life, revered for zeal. Let the righteous love you as a servant of God; let the wicked dread your face as that of a judge. Let no one in your sight presume to do anything alien to good morals, since all know that you cannot tolerate injury done to God. Thus Phinehas earned the everlasting priesthood, when by zealously defending the law he powerfully appeased the wrath of the Lord.

If you see order perishing in the monastery, if your brothers have begun in any way to corrupt regular observance, do not, if you are a servant of God, keep silence about their vices. Set yourself like a wall, bravely, before the house of the Lord; exercise zeal for God as far as you are able; destroy the counsels of the malicious; resist the rashness of the proud. If you are a true lover of God, by your face alone you will scatter the assemblies of the depraved. For no one will disclose his plan before you if he suspects your zeal to be against it. But if the wicked and reprobate do not fear your presence, they plainly recognize no zeal for God in you.

Therefore, to show yourself a true servant of Christ, you must willingly forgive your brothers, for the love of God, the wrongs done to you, and pray to God for those very persons who wrong you. But wrongs done to the Lord are not yours to forgive without his will; rather, out of zeal for uprightness, you must avenge them. In these matters let love of blood-kin cease; let the bond of friendship withdraw far away: zeal for God is rightly to be preferred to all things. For human friendship must be observed in such a way that it is never preferred to zeal for God.

Woe to the monks and abbots who so boldly cast aside zeal for God; who put human familiarities before the divine command; who conceal the vices of their subjects through foolish compassion; who do not observe the traditions of the holy Rule even in others. And what shall I say? We see among cloistered monks obedience to commands despised, zeal for uprightness scorned, observance of the Rule contemned. Two or more contract among themselves a bond of fleshly friendship under the name of charity. The infirm entrust the diseases of their soul to those more infirm, and they hardly seek friendship with God through purity of mind. Each thinks his own companion better than the rest, and each, deceived, loves the other not spiritually but carnally, since they do not lift their affections to God; he loves nothing but the consolations of the flesh.

But the monk whom you see seeking the friendship of infirm brothers you must judge not a servant of God but a lover of the flesh. For the man who truly occupies his whole heart in the love of God cares nothing for human friendship. The love of Jesus suffices him for all things; beyond him he seeks nothing more. But whoever has sought the consolation of his mind in outward things shows by his deed that he does not love God with his whole heart.

The love of God loves solitude, hates the tumult of men, and does not seek conversations with friends. O good Jesus, how sweet is your love, how it pierces the heart that loves you; seeing you, it desires to see you; having you, the soul longs to embrace you.

70

For indeed, he who loves you forgets himself. He meditates on nothing other than your most sweet presence. There is nothing in the world that pleases one who loves you; nowhere is anything found that the soul desires besides you. O, with how many sighs the mind wounded by love is distressed; with what abundant tears the face is watered in secret, because as often as it thinks of the face of the beloved presiding in heaven, so often it bewails itself as desolate on earth. Meanwhile the mind, languishing with love, attempts to say something of its most beloved Jesus; it strives also to stir others to love of him. But as soon as it has begun to utter the most sweet name of Jesus, because of the greatness of love it falls silent against its will. For the love of Jesus is expressed by no words, but is felt with sweetness in the secret of the mind. I know who said: “My love has been crucified.” “Who is your love, O servant of God? Why do you weep? Why do you groan?” “Ignatius. My love has been crucified, and shall I not mourn? My Lord is dead, and shall I be able to restrain my tears?” Do not weep, O faithful soul; for although your love died in order to redeem you from death, nevertheless he has now risen from the dead in order to crown you in heaven. Be faithful unto death, and he will give you the crown of life.

On the manner and seven degrees of divine love, comprising the conclusion of this second region.

Since no one is suddenly made highest, nor can anyone by his own powers suddenly ascend to that very summit of divine love, it is useful now briefly to note the fixed modes or degrees themselves of loving God. Therefore, for moving the human heart to divine love, the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ is in my judgment more effective than all other things, if it has been purely, sweetly, fervently, perseveringly, and diligently pondered in the mind of a human being. For indeed, whoever recalls to memory, with compassion and thanksgiving, the life, Passion, and death of the Savior according to the principal and especially important articles, prepares a swift ascent of the heart to divine love. But we shall treat this most holy occupation of the mind concerning the Lord’s Passion appropriately in the second principal part of this work, where we shall set forth more fully the manner of spiritual exercise. But insofar as the account of what has been said pertains to this place, I find three modes of loving God, which I shall briefly explain in order.

The first mode commands that you love him who loves you sweetly; join yourself wholly to him delightfully, so that your heart loves nothing apart from God and seeks nothing elsewhere. For since God is the whole, he alone desires to possess the whole heart of the lover; he withdraws himself from scattered thoughts. Therefore, if you wish to love sweetly, love totally. For the love of God brings about either everything or nothing. Let meditation on the Passion of Jesus Christ our Savior possess you wholly, until love in you

Prefatio in tertiū trattatum prime partis: qui describit supremam regionē spiritus claustralium. <Initial type="decorated-drop">S</Initial>Cripturꝰ tandē adiuuāte dn̄io supremā illā regionē spiritus: pauore simul et pudore ꝯcutior: qmͣ et parvus loqui de rebꝰ maximis timeo: et docere q̄ nō satꝭ sum exp̄tus multū erubesco: Cuiꝰ em̄ p̄tūlibet exercitati hoīs ingeniiū: statū mētꝭ ꝑ amorē in deo suauiter qͥescētꝭ agnosceret: vl̓qͥs sermo etiā facūdissimi oratorꝭ interne ꝯtēplatōis secretā dulcedinē explicaret? Em̄ uero huiꝰ tertie regionis exercitiū intellectuꝫ humanū ꝓ maiori ꝑte exuꝑat: in quo mens purificati hoīs ꝑ feruorē diuini amori: suꝑ semetip̄am rapit̉: et in abysso diuīe ꝯtēplationis naturali essentia ꝑmanēte mirabili dulcedīe soporata absorbet. Nā tanta suauitate maiestatꝭ interne opp̄mit̉: vt statū suū nec intelligere: nec eloqui posse videat̉. Oꝑatōe siquidē sensitīa deserrena: etiā intellectiuā penitꝰ supergredit̉: et qd̓ est ampliꝰ seip̄am deseꝛmū illū diuīe caligīs verticē ꝑ affectū eleuat̉. Cū d̓o a semetip̄a peneitus defecerit: nō agit sed qͥescit: nec ad se reuersa qͥd fuerit passapōt intelligere nec modū eleuatōis sue alicui reuelare. Tam em̄ ꝓfunda: tamqꝫ sublimis est mentꝭ ista in deū eleuatio: vt eam nō solū inexꝑtus nō possit intelligere: sed neqꝫ expertꝰ etiā quēadmodū ipsa est eam penitꝰ valeat verbꝭ explicare. Ego aut̄ qͥd potero demōte diuīe caligī dicere: quē nec dū merui penetrare? Non decēt stultū verba ꝯposita: nec loqui de secretꝭ diuīecōtēplatōis homo imꝓeritus et rigidus debuit: qͥ cum infirmis adhuc in vallibus consistit.
